The list was on the fridge under a magnet shaped like a lemon. Ruth had written it in March, when their mother could still hold a pen steady: CUPBOARD, DRAWER, FREEZER, and then, underlined twice, MUST NOT BE SPLIT.

"It's a spoon," Dan said.

"It's the spoon." Ruth held it up. The wood had gone pale and soft on one side of the bowl, where years of stirring had rubbed it down. "She stirred the tomato sauce with that for thirty years. Nobody else touched it."

"You can't split a spoon."

"I'm not splitting it. I'm saying I want it."

Dan opened the freezer and looked at the bags, each labelled in their mother's square capitals. PEAS. PEAS. BROTH (GOOD). He read the dates aloud, as if they settled something. Jan. Feb. Two thousand and nine.

"Those are older than your job," Ruth said.

"Those are still food."

"Nobody is eating that."

He shut the drawer. "Fine. Spoon's yours. The pan."

"You don't want the pan."

"I want the pan because you want the pan."

They stood with the cupboard open between them. The cheap plates had a crack in one, which neither of them mentioned. On the counter, the kettle was still full from the morning, because neither of them had remembered to switch it on.

"She'd have given us the spoon to fight over," Dan said. "And then she'd have stolen it back."

Ruth laughed, and it came out wrong, a cough. She handed him the pan. He took it. Then she turned the spoon over, found the good side, the one that had never been worn down, and kept that side facing up as she put it in her coat pocket.

"You're wrecking the system," Dan said.

"It's my system now."

The lemon magnet slid off the fridge and hit the floor. Neither of them picked it up.

Danny's mum said the same thing every night: "Brush your teeth, and don't let me hear a peep."

And every night, Danny heard a peep.

It came from the drawer of his bedside table. A tiny sound, like a spoon tapped on a glass, twice, then a pause.

The first week, he told his mum. She opened the drawer. Socks. A torch with no batteries. A birthday card from his gran. Nothing that tapped.

The second week, he told his friend Priya.

"That's a ghost," said Priya, chewing her pencil. "Ghosts rattle things. You have to say, *What do you want?*"

So that night, Danny turned off the light, lay very still, and whispered, "What do you want?"

The tapping stopped. Then a voice, thin as a thread, said, "My marble."

Danny sat up. "What?"

"My marble. The blue one. I was keeping it in there and then the drawer got emptied and now I can't find it anywhere, and I've looked for a very long time."

Danny switched on his lamp. He looked at the drawer. He looked at the floor. He looked under the bed, where things went when they were lost on purpose.

Behind the bedpost, in a grey fluff the hoover never reached, he found it. A blue glass marble, small as a pea, with a white twist inside.

The voice made a sound like a held breath going out.

Danny put the marble back in the drawer and closed it.

"Thank you," said the voice. "I'll be quiet now."

And it was.

Danny lay in the dark for a while, thinking about a person who had lost one marble and had been worrying about it for years and years.

The next night, before he turned off the light, he put something else in the drawer, just in case. A red marble from his own collection.

In the morning, it was still there.

But it had moved to the corner of the drawer, as if someone had set it down carefully after looking at it.

Cold Storage

The lost-and-found office at Terminal 2 has no windows and no chairs, so people stand at the counter the way they stand at a wake, hands folded, saying the same sentence in different orderings. Nadia has worked the counter eleven years. She knows the sentence before they say it.

The receipts get written in triplicate. The property is tagged and shelved by date, then by size, then by anything that makes it findable. A wheelchair waiting on the shelf line, someone's laptop, a single ski, a box of someone else's mother.

What comes in most is the shape a person leaves behind when they run. Belts at security, always belts. Coats. Shoes off in a tub and never claimed. Once a wooden leg.

The shelf labels are her handwriting. She writes small.

There's a rule about unclaimed property after ninety days. Auction, or destruction, depending. She is the one who decides which is which. She has been wrong. She has been right. There's no way to tell which is which until later, and by later she is not in the room anymore.

On the shelf this week: a single sock in a plastic bag, a pair of reading glasses still warm, a package with x-ray tape on all four sleeves and a return address in a town with two syllables and nothing else. A stuffed rabbit, one ear. A silver flask, empty.

She does not open the flask. That is not the rule. There is no rule about the flask. She does not open the flask.

A man comes in at 4:40 in the afternoon. He has been walking through the terminal for two hours and is still wearing his coat. He says the sentence. She asks the questions on the form: description, date lost, terminal, flight number. He does not have the flight number. He has a piece of paper with a scribble on it that turns out to be the flight number, and the scribble was in his own handwriting, from before the airport lost him.

She looks on the shelf. The tag is there. The item is there. She brings it to the counter and sets it down, and he does not touch it. He just stands. She has seen people do this before. The object exists on both sides of a loss for a moment, and then the loss comes back, and it's the same shape, but the object is now in front of them and the loss is not.

He signs. She files. The door closes, and the office is even and quiet.

The boards overhead change every few minutes. The flights leave whether anyone is on them. She has a cup of coffee on the desk that stopped being hot an hour ago. She drinks it anyway. On the shelf, the tags sit in a row, and the row keeps getting longer, and no one has ever come back for the flask.

The lost-property office at Harrow Field closes at ten, but Dolores stays until the last flight from Leeds is logged. Her shelf is a sorting of who left in a hurry.

A child's left shoe, still tied. A passport photo of a man with his hair cut for it. Three umbrellas, which means it rained somewhere else.

She writes the tags in pencil because the ink pen skips on cold mornings. Date, terminal, gate. Where found. Under "description," she tries to be exact without being cruel: *grey cardigan, one button missing.* Someone will read it in a parked car and know it's theirs.

Most people don't come back. She has learned not to take it personally. A lost thing is often just a thing that got left at the moment someone had to choose which hand to use for the bags.

At 9:52 a woman in a green coat asks about a phone charger. Dolores finds one in a tray, cable coiled, adaptor still taped. The woman looks at it as if it might bite.

"Is this yours?"

"No," the woman says. "Mine was in my other bag. Can I have this one anyway?"

Dolores hands it over and writes *charger, taped, collected by owner, 9:53*, which is almost true.

A child's left shoe, still tied. A passport photo of a man with his hair cut for it. Three umbrellas, which means it rained somewhere else.

At 9:52 a woman in a green coat asks about a phone charger. Dolores finds one in a tray, cable coiled, adaptor still taped. The woman looks at it as if it might bite.

"No," the woman says. "Mine was in my other bag. Can I have this one anyway?"

Dolores hands it over and writes *charger, taped, collected by owner, 9:53*, which is almost true.

My cousin Reenie moved into a flat above a chip shop, and the first night she heard it: someone downstairs sweeping.

Slow, steady sweeps. Brush, brush, brush. Then a pause, the way you pause to gather a pile, then sweeping again. It went on past midnight. Reenie knocked on the floor. The sweeping stopped. She lay back down. It started again, right under her bed.

The chip shop shut at nine. Nobody was down there.

Night two, same thing. Night three, she counted. Forty-one sweeps, then the pause, then forty-one more.

She got a torch and went down. The shop was dark and smelled of old oil. No broom. The floor was clean, and every chair was stacked on its table, all of them, like always.

She stood still and listened. From above her own flat, she heard sweeping. She ran up. Nothing. Downstairs again — sweeping. It moved whichever place she was not.

Her nan told her what to do. Don't go looking, she said. Don't ask it to stop. Just sweep back.

So the next night Reenie got the yard broom and swept her own kitchen floor, slow, brush, brush, brush, and when she paused, the sound below her paused too. She swept again. It answered. Back and forth, all night, two floors sweeping at each other.

It still comes. Most nights she sweeps a bit before bed, and it sweeps along with her, and then it stops, and she sleeps fine.

But here is the thing she told me, and she made me promise not to laugh.

It doesn't want the floor clean. She's checked. It's never once asked her to stop.

It just wants someone else in the building who knows how to sweep.

The lost-property shelf at Gate 14 held a single umbrella, a child's left shoe, and a box of wax lips that had been there since March. Teodora logged each item on a card and tied the card to the handle with string. Nobody had ever come back for the wax lips. She kept them anyway, because the card was printed on the back of an old boarding pass and that felt like enough.

On a Tuesday in October a man in a grey coat stood at the counter with his passport open to the wrong page. He said he was looking for a thermos. Green, dented on one side, with a strip of masking tape on the lid that said RAMON in capitals.

She did not have a thermos. She said so. He nodded as if he had expected that and set his bag down.

"I left it in 2009," he said. "Seat 22C, the flight to Lisbon. I went back to get it and they had already taken it away."

"Then it went to the bins, probably."

"I know. I wanted to ask anyway."

She looked at the shelf behind her. Eleven items that week. None of them green. She turned back to him and asked what had been in the thermos.

He thought about it. Coffee, he said, but the cold kind, the kind you make the night before. He had made it for his father, who used to drive him to the airport on school trips and who had stopped driving the year after. He did not explain why the thermos mattered and she did not ask.

"I'll write it down," she said. "If it turns up."

He wrote his name and a number on the back of her card. Then he went through security without his bag, because she had already told the next officer he could.

The card stayed in the tray for three weeks. On the twenty-second of November a cleaner found a green thermos in the seating area of Gate 9, under a row of chairs, the masking tape on the lid worn nearly through. Teodora read the name and the date on the card, put the two together, and carried the thermos to the desk.

She didn't call the number. She put the thermos on the shelf between the umbrella and the wax lips, and wrote a new card, and tied it on with string.

Lost property at Gate Area Dock C is a windowless room behind a steel door that says STAFF ONLY in two languages, one of them crossed out with tape.

Marisol works the counter from six to two. She has a rule about the things that come in: she logs them, she bags them, she does not wonder. Wondering takes too long and the shelves fill up.

On Tuesday a man brings in a single left shoe, brown, cracked at the heel. He says he was on the 9:40 to Pamplona. He does not say why he needs the shoe back or why he didn't have the other one with him. She asks him to describe it. He does, in more detail than she needs, and then he says, "The lace is the wrong color. I bought them that way on purpose."

She writes it down. Shoe, left, brown, lace wrong color, claimant: M. Oyelaran. She puts it on the third shelf between a child's rain boot and a cake box with no cake in it.

On Thursday a woman sends her husband up to ask if they have a wind-up frog. They do not. They have a wind-up frog's cousin, a wind-up duck, which the husband looks at, sighs, and takes. Marisol doesn't know if that was the right frog.

The rule is easier when the things are dumb objects. A dentures case is a dentures case. A passport with someone else's face is only a passport with a face. She can hold anything for thirty days and then send it to the auction in Coventry, where it gets a number and a price and goes home with someone who will never know.

Except the film canister. It came in last spring, rattling, from a seat in row nineteen. Inside: a ring, thin, worn to almost nothing on one side from years of turning. No note. Marisol tipped it onto the counter and it rolled a little, the way rings do, and stopped against the edge of the register, and she stood there longer than the rule allows.

She logged it. She bagged it. The auction sent back the envelope in August marked UNCLAIMED, and she was surprised, a little, by how much she had wanted it to go somewhere.

Today the bell over the steel door chimes at 1:58. A woman comes up to the counter, out of breath, one hand on her coat pocket.

"I think I left something on the plane," she says.

"Describe it," Marisol says, and reaches for the pen.

The Boy Who Was Always Called In

My aunt lived in a flat above a chip shop, and I slept on the sofa for two weeks one summer. Every night at half past nine I heard a door click in the hallway.

Nobody used the hallway. It was just a passage with coats on hooks and a bike that never moved.

Click. Pause. Three steps. Pause. Then the creak of the front door, and nothing.

I asked my aunt. She didn't look up from the potatoes. "That's the boy," she said. "He's being called in for his tea."

I said there wasn't a boy.

"He doesn't know that," she said.

So the next night I sat in the hallway with the light off. Half past nine. Click. Three steps — small steps, a kid's steps, the kind that drag a bit on the heel.

Then a voice from down the stairwell, a woman's voice, ordinary as anything: "Your tea's going cold!"

And the front door opened by itself, just a hand's width, and stayed.

I didn't see a boy. I want to be honest about that. I saw the door move, and I heard the steps, and I heard the woman. That's all.

The next night I sat there again. Same thing. And the night after.

Here's the part I still think about. On my last night, at half past nine, the door clicked. The three steps came. And the woman's voice said, "Your tea's going cold."

But this time it wasn't coming up the stairwell.

It was coming from inside the flat.

I went to bed after that. I didn't tell my aunt. And when I left in the morning she waved from the window and said, "Come back next summer, he'll be glad of the company."

The Lamp at Hollin Bridge

Every night at nine, the lamp on Hollin Bridge flickered on, though nobody lived in the mill cottage that owned it.

Priya and her little brother Sam were allowed to walk as far as the bridge, but never past it. Their gran said that was where the Lamp Lady lived.

"Why does she only come out at nine?" asked Sam, clutching a torch he wasn't allowed to switch on yet.

"Because she's shy," said Priya, who had decided this was true. "She only waves when she thinks no one's watching."

That night they crept out, Sam in his dressing gown, Priya with her coat buttoned wrong. The lamp was already glowing. Under it, in the middle of the bridge, stood a small figure in a grey shawl, holding something up to the light.

It was a jar. Inside the jar, a tiny blue flame was turning slow circles, like a fish.

The figure looked up. Her face was kind and crinkled, like paper that has been folded many times.

"You're the children from the top house," she said. "Your gran told me you'd come one day. She said you'd want to know why the lamp is lit."

"Why is it?" whispered Sam.

"Because someone has to light it," said the Lamp Lady, "so that anyone lost in the fog can find their way home. Tonight, I think, you two found your way here."

She held out the jar. Priya did not take it, but she leaned close. The flame warmed her cheeks, and for a moment she heard her gran's voice calling from far away, saying supper was ready.

When she opened her eyes, the bridge was just a bridge, and the lamp was just a lamp, and the figure was gone.

Sam was already running home. Priya followed, and when she looked back, the light was still burning, steady as a heartbeat.

Her gran was at the door with the torch in her hand. "You went to the bridge," she said. It wasn't a question.

"Yes," said Priya. "She's not so scary. She's just very busy."

He was standing in aisle four when he said it, holding the wrench up like a small silver fish, and I was nine and didn't understand that he was talking about anything but wrenches. That was thirty-one years ago. The closing-out sign came down from the attic last Tuesday, still creased from the last time it was used, when Grandpa sold the lumberyard to the Biddles in '78, and we hung it in the window between the fly strips and the hand-lettered card that says NO BOLTS SOLD SINGLE. The bolts are still sold single. The sign is going back up tomorrow.

The Lighthouse Keeper's Cat

On the cliffs above Gullhaven there was a lighthouse, and in the lighthouse lived a cat named Ferris who had never once been afraid of anything.

Ferris was not afraid of the foghorn, or the wind that rattled the shutters, or the crabs that scuttled across the rocks below. So when the little girl from the cottage up the hill began to visit the lighthouse each evening, Ferris only blinked at her and went back to sleep.

"Are you a ghost?" she asked him one night.

Ferris yawned. Cats do not usually answer questions.

"Everybody says there's a ghost up here," she whispered. "A sailor who came in on the storm and never went out again."

Ferris stretched, walked to the window, and looked out at the black water. Something pale was standing on the rocks below, very still, facing the light.

The girl came and stood beside him. "Oh," she said softly. "He's waiting for someone to bring him home."

Ferris looked at her, then at the sea, then back at the girl.

Then he did something no cat in Gullhaven had ever done. He jumped onto the lamp's brass rail, walked along it as if it were a fence in the garden, and rang the little bell three times.

Down on the rocks, the pale shape turned, and faded into the fog like morning mist, and was gone.

"Thank you," the girl said.

Ferris sat down, licked one paw, and went back to sleep. Some things, he had decided long ago, were better handled with a bit of ringing and no fuss at all.

The Lamp at Hollow Creek Bridge

Nobody in Pennick Cove went near the old bridge after dark. Everyone said so, and nobody could say why.

Mina was ten, and she did not believe in things like that. So when her brother dared her to walk across at midnight and count the lamps, she laughed and said yes.

The lamp posts stood along the bridge, one every ten steps, and each one had a small glass lantern on top. Mina started counting. One. Two. Three. At the fourth lamp, the light was off. At the fifth, it was off too.

By the sixth lamp, she could hear someone humming behind her.

She did not turn around. Her grandmother had taught her that. "If something hums behind you on a bridge, keep walking and keep counting," Grandma had said. "Don't answer, and don't look."

So Mina counted. Seven. Eight. The humming came closer, soft and tuneless, like someone who had forgotten the words.

At the ninth lamp, a cold hand touched her shoulder.

"You're counting wrong," said a small voice. "There are ten lamps. You skipped one."

Mina stopped. She did not look. "Which one did I skip?"

"The one you walked past when you were little," said the voice. "You dropped your red mitten there. You never went back for it."

Mina thought hard. She remembered the mitten. She had cried all the way home. She had never known who took it.

"Is that you?" she whispered.

"It was," said the voice. "I kept it warm for you."

The humming stopped. The tenth lamp flickered on, bright and yellow. Mina looked at it, and her heart did a strange, sad little turn.

At the foot of the lamp post lay a red mitten, folded neatly, as if someone had set it down with care.

Mina picked it up. It was still warm.

She walked the rest of the bridge slowly, counting every lamp out loud, all ten of them. When she reached the far end, she looked back. The bridge was empty and quiet.

But the lamps were all shining.

And somewhere out on the water, a small voice said, "Thank you for counting."

But the lamps were all shining.

And somewhere out on the water, a small voice said, "Thank you for counting."
</final>

My sister asked me to be the one who held things. Not a bridesmaid, not a witness — she said, "Just carry the folder," so I carried the folder: both birth certificates, the license, the two rings in a ziplock because she did not trust the box.

The office was on the second floor, above a currency exchange. Fluorescent light, a dying ficus, a laminated sign about no food or drink. Twelve of us in folding chairs. The clerk had a cold and a lanyard that read DANILO, and Danilo had, it turned out, been given the wrong date in the system. Thursday, not Tuesday. He found this out while holding my sister's birth certificate up to the window light as if he could see the mistake in it.

"You're not on today's list," he said.

We had the room until eleven. The next couple was at nine-thirty, already standing by the door in matching cream, the woman holding a small bouquet by its stems like a torch.

I want to say we handled it well. What happened was that my mother started crying in the way that makes strangers offer help, and the security guard, who had been upstairs for eleven years, said he'd seen the supervisor fix this before, and then there was a phone call, and then there was a second phone call, and then we all just stood in the corridor for forty minutes while the cream couple went in and came out married, throwing nothing, because there was no one to throw rice and also a sign.

My sister sat on the floor with her back against the wall. That's the part I keep coming back to. Not the dress — she'd worn a green dress she already owned, which she'd bought for a funeral the year before and liked the pockets of. She sat on the linoleum in that dress and did not cry and did not say anything for a while, and then she asked me for the folder, and checked, quietly, one by one, that every paper was still there.

They got married at two-forty. Two witnesses, a different clerk, a room with the blinds half down. It took nine minutes. Danilo came and stood at the back even though nothing required him to, and sneezed twice, and left before the photos.

Afterward we went to the café downstairs because it was raining and nobody wanted to walk. My brother-in-law ate a toastie. My mother had tea and stopped crying somewhere around the second cup. My sister put the ziplock of rings on the table between the sugar and the napkin holder, and we sat there a while, all of us, watching the exchange place across the street change numbers on its board.

The folder stayed on my lap the whole time. She never asked for it back. I have it now, in the drawer with the takeaway menus, and I'm not going to be the one who brings it up first.

The ring went on fine. That was the part everyone had practiced.

What went wrong was the uncle.

Dermot had come over on the Thursday boat and stayed in the box room, and on the morning of it he was up before anyone, sitting in the kitchen with his good shoes already on and both hands flat on the table like a man waiting for a verdict. Marie's mother gave him tea. He said the tea was good and then said nothing else for a long time, which in that house was close to an alarm.

The ceremony was at eleven. The church held about ninety and there were a hundred and four. People stood at the back against the wall where the plaster was cold and the stations of the cross had gone grey. Marie came up the aisle with her brother, who had a dry-cleaning tag hanging from the cuff of his jacket and no idea. She didn't notice. She was watching the altar, or the window over it, or something past both.

The priest was new and read their names slightly wrong.

They got through it. Vows, rings, the small shuffle when the photographer wants the kiss from a second angle. Outside, the light was doing that thing it does in that flat county in October, all silver, no shadows, everything the same brightness so you can't tell what time it is. The cousins had confetti in a plastic bag from a shop that had closed years ago. It said Fun Time on the bag. Somebody read it out and laughed.

The dinner was in the hall. Chicken or beef, the tickets collected by a girl of about fifteen who took the job seriously and would not be hurried. Dermot was put at the top table because he was the oldest and the mother had arranged it to make a point about something that had happened in 1994. He ate about half. He drank water.

The speech came. Marie's father stood up and got through three sentences and stopped. Not because he was moved. Because he had lost it — the whole thing, the page he'd written it on, which was in the car, and the car keys were in the car, which was noticed only later. He said a few words about weather. He said Marie had been a good child and was now a good woman, which she heard, and which she thought about for years afterward, in different rooms, with the door shut.

Then Dermot stood up.

Nobody expected it. He wasn't on the list. He held the table edge with both hands, the way he'd held the table in the morning, and said he wanted to say one thing about the family, and then said the thing. It wasn't cruel and it wasn't a secret. It was worse than that. It was true, and it was about the grandmother, and about who had paid for what, and about a debt that everyone in the room had grown up inside of without ever being told its name, and he said it in the flat voice of a man reading out a bus timetable.

The band, which had been setting up at the side, put down the lead and went outside for a smoke.

Marie didn't cry. She looked at the tables, at the uncle, at the plates with the dessert on them, lemon posset in little glasses with a mint leaf on each, and she thought, clearly and without heat: I will remember this until I die, and it will not be the wedding.

Someone got the band back in. The first dance happened. People danced.

At about one in the morning Dermot was gone, back to the box room or the boat, and the hall was being swept, and one of the young lads was stacking chairs with enormous care, folding each one and setting it down like it was worth money, which at that hour it nearly was.

The trouble started with a hyphen.

Mira and Tom had been standing at the counter of the registry office since nine. The building was a low brick thing near the river with a portrait of a president who'd been out of office six years. Two rubber plants, one of them dying. Outside the window, a barge pushed past, gray on gray.

"I have her as Halvorsen," said the clerk behind the glass. "Without the bend in the middle."

"Halvorsen-Sand," Mira said. "Both our names. We filed in September."

The clerk went away and came back with a folder. She was not cruel about it; she was just a person at the end of a long queue of people who wanted things. The register said Mira Halvorsen. Tom had no middle name to join to hers. Their application had dissolved somewhere between the person who took it and the person who typed it, and now the typed version was the true one.

"You can be married today as Halvorsen," the clerk said. "Or in three weeks as Halvorsen-Sand."

Tom's parents were in the hallway with a thermos and a plate of butter cookies going soft. Mira's were driving in from four hours away and had already, at that moment, turned onto the bridge.

Mira looked at the pen chained to the counter.

She thought about the invitations she had printed herself, thirty of them, a frog in the corner of each one because Tom had proposed at the pond behind his mother's house and they had neither of them been able to think of anything better. She thought about the cake in the trunk of the car, which was not a cake but six trays of a rice pudding her aunt made for occasions, because the aunt had said once, in front of everyone, that she would make it the day Mira married, and had been saying it since Mira was eleven. The trays were in the trunk in a cooler bag, and it was about two degrees out, so it was fine.

"Halvorsen," Mira said.

Tom said, "What?"

"You can be a Sand after. It's a suffix. It can wait."

"It's my name too," Tom said, quietly, which is how he said most things.

"It's a hyphen," Mira said. "It's a little stick between letters. We can have it in three weeks."

So they did it as Halvorsen. The clerk read the words, they repeated, Tom's mother cried a small efficient amount, and the barge went and came back with its friend. The hallway smelled of wet wool and the cookies and the dying rubber plant.

Afterward they walked to the river while the parents sorted out cars. There was ice along the edge, a thin brown crust the barges had chewed up and the cold was knitting back.

"We still have to do it again," Tom said.

"I know."

"In three weeks. Just us. Sign the thing."

"Twice," Mira said. "Some people do worse."

Tom took the cooler bag from her without being asked, which was a thing he did, and they stood and watched the water until Tom's mother called to them that they'd parked her in, and Mira had to go move the car.

They married in the third week of December and again in the second week of January, and the marriage certificate they framed and hung by the door was the second one, which had the hyphen, and which was, by then, worth the wait.

They kept the pool dry on purpose. Not for the tiles or the echo, but because Odile could read a person's water in the air down there. The old filtration room held the cold from whenever the water had last been, and the body walking in would either carry enough of it to fog a breath on the handrail or it wouldn't. The ferry had been stuck on the far bank since eleven, and by two the groom's mother had stopped pretending to read the seating chart.

"They'll come on the next crossing," said Ruta, who ran the ticket hut and had said so four times.

The next crossing was at four. Nobody could say what would be different about four.

The bride's family was on the boat. So were the flowers, the cake in its three tiers wrapped in damp towels, and her grandmother, who had insisted on coming because she had been married on that same ferry in 1961 and did not trust the new cable. Across the brown water the church bell rang the hour anyway, as if the town had decided the wedding would happen with or without anybody in it.

Tomas, the groom, stood at the slip with his good shoes going dark at the toes. He had not slept. His cousin kept offering him a cigarette he did not want.

"There's the ford," the cousin said.

Everyone in the town knew about the ford. It ran shallow in late summer, a line of gravel under a skin of water, and for forty years it had been forbidden, after a tractor went under and a boy with it. People still crossed it on dares. Old men crossed it to prove they still could.

"No," said Tomas's mother.

"Nobody's asking you."

"I'm asking you not to be a fool."

The grandmother's voice came across the water, thin but carrying, because she had spent a lifetime shouting over engines. She was not calling for help. She was telling them the water was at the third post, which meant it was too high for gravel and not high enough to be safe, which was the only thing anybody needed to hear.

Tomas walked to the edge of the slip and looked. He could see the bride, small and dark against the rail, one hand up to her veil. She was not waving. She was counting, the way she always did when she was nervous, and he could tell from her shoulders which number she had reached.

He took off his shoes.

Behind him someone said his name in the voice people use for funerals. He did not turn around. The gravel was cold through his socks. The first step went down to his shin, the second to his knee, and then the current leaned on him gently, the way a crowd leans on a door it has decided to open.

He stopped. The water was brown and fast and smelled of cut grass. On the far bank, the bride had stopped counting.

Ruta came down the slip with a rope over her shoulder, the one she used for tying up the ferry on stormy nights, and threw one end toward him. It fell short, then fell right.

"Hold it," she said. "Don't be brave. Hold it."

He held it.

Across the water, the bride unclipped her veil and handed it to her grandmother, who took it without a word and tucked it into her coat. Then the bride stepped to the rail, looked at the ford, and started counting again.

The pipes were always going to outlast us. That was the mistake nobody wanted to name: we built the city around them, and then we let them become the city.

Mira had been walking the Line for eleven years. The Line was forty kilometers of main, laid before the towers went up, back when the engineers still believed the river would keep its side of the bargain. It ran beneath the eastern districts, under the markets and the laundry lines and the block where Mira's mother had kept a key in a tin box above the door.

The key was gone. The door was gone. The block was a slope of rubble that the wind rearranged each week, and Mira walked over it twice a year on her way to the pumps, and did not slow down.

Her job, on paper, was inspection. She carried a wrench, a lamp, and a ledger her predecessor had started in a hand she had learned to read the way you learn a relative's handwriting — slowly, and with guesses. The ledger said the Line had twenty-three valves. Mira had found twenty-two. The twenty-third was somewhere under the eastern slope, and she had stopped looking for it around year four, and had never written that down.

Water still moved in the Line. Not much. What moved was old, dark, and tasted of iron and the inside of a jar. It seeped down from the north field where the snowmelt used to be, and it arrived at the pumps in a trickle that filled a bucket in an hour. Enough to drink. Not enough to wash. The city had agreed on that, once, in a meeting Mira had attended. Everyone would drink. No one would wash. The agreement had lasted longer than anyone expected, mostly because the alternative was to admit they could have done it differently, ten years back, when the reservoir was low but not empty, and the council had chosen to keep the fountains running one more summer for the tourists who were not coming.

Mira did not hate the council. She had stopped bothering.

At the pump house she opened the ledger and wrote the date, and then, under it, the pressure, which was the same as last month. She capped the pen. The lamp made a circle on the wall that was the only warm thing for a kilometer.

There was a sound. Not the wind. Metal, settling. She went outside and stood on the concrete apron and listened, and it came again, from the ground, from the Line, deep and slow, the way a big animal breathes in a story.

She knew the sound. She had heard it once, as a girl, on a field trip her school had taken to see the reservoir when there was still water in it. The reservoir had been letting go of a seam. The engineers had called it breathing and told the children it was nothing.

Mira stood on the apron and listened to the Line breathe. Twenty-two valves. The twenty-third was under the eastern slope, and if it was opening, then somewhere below her a quantity of water she could not picture was deciding where to go.

She went back inside and sat down. She wrote the pressure again, in a different column, so that whoever read the ledger next would know she had heard it and had not run.

In the morning she would walk east. She would dig where the slope was softest, and she would find the valve, or she would not, and either way she would come back and write it down. The city behind her would wake and line up at the pumps with their buckets and their jars, and they would not know that anything had changed, and she would not tell them, because she did not yet know herself, and because there was no meeting left that would matter.

She turned the lamp down. The Line breathed under the rubble, patient, in no hurry, the way a thing is patient when it has been holding something for a very long time and has finally been asked a question.

The ring went missing at 4:10, twenty minutes before the bride was due to walk down the aisle between the Hereford pens.

Dolores found out because she was the one holding it. She had been told to keep it in her left shoe, which was the old way, and then she had taken the shoe off to stand on the cold concrete while the florist pinned a carnation to her cardigan. When she bent to put the shoe back on, the ring was gone. It had not rolled under anything. It was in a bucket of pellets by the goat stall, where a six-year-old named Tate had put it because it was shiny.

"It's a good ring," Tate said. He held out his palm. "I was going to give it back."

The bride, Renee, did not cry. She had decided on the drive over that she would not cry in a barn, and she had kept to it through the planning, the seating chart, the fight about the cake. Now she stood in her dress with pellet dust on the hem and said nothing at all, which her mother said was worse.

The groom, Alan, was already a little sunburned from the morning in the parking field. He asked if they could use the plastic ring from the cereal box, the one Tate had won in March. Everyone in the barn heard him say it. Renee's mother made a sound like a kettle.

Grandmother Iris had not spoken since the buses arrived. She was ninety-one, and she had worn the same dove-gray dress to every wedding in the family since 1958. She walked over to the goat stall with her cane, leaned her weight on the rail, and looked at the bucket.

"Nobody touches it," she said. "Bring me a clean towel."

They brought her a clean towel from the first-aid kit. She knelt, which took three people, and sorted through the pellets with her fingers, slowly, the way she shelled peas. It took eleven minutes. The DJ kept playing the same song at a low volume, because no one had told him to stop. A goat chewed on Alan's boutonniere.

When Iris stood up, she had the ring in the palm of her hand and a pellet stuck to her thumb. She wiped the ring on the towel, then wiped it again, then held it out to Renee without a word.

Renee took it. Her hands were shaking now, and that was when she finally cried, not hard, just enough to make her mascara run in two straight lines. She laughed at herself for it. Alan put his arm around her and said something that made her laugh more.

"Forty years ago my husband lost mine in the stock tank," Iris said to nobody in particular. "Sank to the bottom. We waited for the draining. Then he dropped a fresh one in the middle of the vows and I said yes anyway." She picked a pellet off her sleeve. "Start the music again. Somebody get that goat away from the boutonniere."

The ceremony began six minutes late. The florist had pinned the carnation back on Dolores's cardigan. Tate walked the aisle ahead of the bride, carrying the cereal-box ring on a pillow, which he had insisted on and which nobody had the heart to stop.

When the officiant asked for the rings, Renee took the real one from her grandmother's towel and slid it on. It was still a little damp. Nobody mentioned it.

The city went dry in the last week of April, and the towers stopped running.

I know that's not the official date. I'm a plumber, not a clerk. The official date is in the third week of May, when the council stopped pretending the pump could still reach the deep aquifer. I remember the dry end of April because that's when the fat ran out.

The city's pipes still had water. That's the part nobody outside understands. The mains were wet. The reservoirs were low but not empty. The problem was the fat. The fat bed is the city's real system — the vaults under the fairgrounds where the old boilers pull the water from the bodies of anyone who gets rendered. The fat is what keeps the pressure up. The fat is what we flush. When the fat ran out, the mains lost pressure, and the last spoke of the city went tight.

I was an apprentice then. My master, Okonkwo, got the call for the fairgrounds, and he sent me with a hand truck and a list. That list was the last honest file in the city. No addresses, just pipe sizes, and a note for each: "one story, two-family, no fat." I carried it to the vaults. The vaults were cool, which was a lie. What was cool in there was the fat. It's a slurry, beige and lumpy, and it smells like a butcher's sink but sweeter.

We worked in the vaults for three days. We're not heroes. We're service. We pulled a family of four out of the fairgrounds in the first week, and the fat is what the pipes carry. That's the system. The pipes are the water's road, but the fat is the water. The body was the source.

When the fat ran out, the city got quiet. The pipes stopped their hum. The tanks stopped their low rumble. The tower stood empty for a month. When the rain comes, we'll be ready. The rain is the new fat. It's the new water. It's in the sky, it's in the pipes, and all we have to do is wait for the first storm. We'll be maintenance. We'll be service.

The city will never be a water city again. It's a fat city. Every city is a fat city. The only question is whether the fat is in the body or in the ground.

The last call was in the fairgrounds. The vaults were empty, the pipes were dry. The tower stood up through the rain, and the rain came down and ran down the pipes. The rain came down the pipes and into the fairgrounds, and the fairgrounds was a lake, and the lake was where the fat was supposed to be.

I wrote in the log: "System ready. First rain." In the morning, the call came in.

The ferry leaves at 4:10 and comes back at 5:40, and everyone in Kilcrane knows that, which is why the vicar asked Dora's father to move the service to two o'clock.

He did not move it. Dora's father had run the crossing for thirty-one years and did not see why a wedding should change the boat.

So the service started at three, which was late for a Saturday and early for the wind. Dora came up the aisle in her mother's shoes, two sizes too big, with a folded tissue stuffed in the left one. Her groom, Neil, cried before she reached him. Everyone agreed later that it was the best bit.

The taps in Veldmark stopped coughing in March. Nobody made a speech about it. Mrs. Osei on the fourth floor noticed first, because she had kept a chair by the kitchen sink for thirty-one years so she could hear the pipes wake up, and one morning they didn't.

The city still had water. It came up from the reservoir at Carrow Hill like always, in the same grey pressure. It just arrived thinner each day, and at a different hour, because somebody upstream had started sharing the pumps by lottery and nobody liked the lottery.

So people learned the new schedule the way they learned weather. The bakery on Lind Street ran its ovens only when the water came, since the steam was water too. The school across the road rang its bell eleven minutes late now, to match the morning fill. Mr. Haddad, who had repaired boilers for forty years, started carrying a plastic jug up and down the stairs at six, and by June the whole block knew his jug's knock on the landing.

Mrs. Osei kept the chair. Her grandson asked her once why, since she could just stand.

"Because I want to be sitting when it comes back," she said, and he did not know if she meant the water or the sound.

It came back in the autumn, at about four in the morning, with a hiss through the walls that woke everyone at once. Nobody cheered. Mr. Haddad put the jug down on the landing and stood there in his socks, listening, until the sound settled into the ordinary knock of the old pipes.

Then he went back inside and slept until seven.

The whetstone lived in the drawer with the rubber bands and the dead batteries, and Bap didn't let anyone else touch it. It was gray, dished in the middle from years of use, and when he set it on the counter he put a folded towel under it so it wouldn't walk.

He took my hands the first time, which he had never done before, and pressed my fingertips flat to the blade.

"Feel that," he said. "That's the burr. That's what you're making."

I couldn't feel anything. I said so. He said, "Then you're not done."

So I went back to it, the blade angled, pushing away from me, the water going gray on the stone. My wrists ached. The kitchen smelled like wet metal. He stood at the window the whole time not looking at me, which was how I knew he was listening.

When I finally got the burr, I almost missed it — a roughness you'd mistake for a scratch. I looked up. He still wasn't looking.

"Again," he said. "Other side."

The knife cut paper after that. He didn't say anything about it. He just took it and put it back in the block and shut the drawer, and I went and found another one.

The meter on the fourth floor of Kell Tower still read 0.00, and Ilse had been checking it every morning for nineteen days, the way some people check a pulse.

The city had not run dry all at once. It had gone the way a sink goes, a little less each week, until the pressure dropped to a thread and then to a drip. The council had sent letters. The letters said *allocation*. Each household got eleven liters a day, measured at the street valve, and the valves were locked with a brass tag stamped with the building's number.

Ilse's tag said 4F. Nobody had come to unlock it.

On the twentieth morning she went down with a bucket and a wrench she had borrowed from the super, who was not using it. The street valve sat in a concrete box under a grate that smelled of wet pennies. Someone had painted a small blue arrow on the lid, pointing east, toward the old reservoir road. Someone else had crossed it out in red.

The tag was not even a lock. It was a plate wired to a clip, and the clip was seated on a bolt that had rusted through at the thread. She turned it with two fingers. It came off like a cap.

Water did not gush. It rose, slowly, the way breath comes back to a sleeper, and filled the bucket to the handle.

She stood there longer than she needed to, watching it settle. Then she heard footsteps on the stairs of the box, and a woman's voice from above said, "Is that yours?"

Ilse looked up. The woman was holding a clipboard and a bottle with no label.

"It's 4F's," Ilse said.

"Right." The woman glanced at the open valve, then at the bucket, then at the rusted bolt, and she wrote something down. "The Thursday audit is at ten. Put the tag back on before then, or they'll fine the building for tampering."

"It broke."

"I know. I'm the one who'll write that down." She tapped the clipboard. "Eleven liters, same as everyone. Your bucket's about nine."

Ilse did not argue. She took the bucket up four flights, one careful step at a time, and set it on the kitchen counter, where the light from the window lay across it like a sheet of glass.

The meter on the wall still said 0.00.

Nana could fold a fitted sheet. Nobody else in the family could, and this was, in her view, not a matter of talent but of paying attention.

She did it on the kitchen table, always the same table, first thing Saturday after the wash. She shook the sheet out and it cracked like a flag. Then corners into corners, the elastic mouths biting each other, her thumbs finding the seams the way you'd find a light switch in your own hallway.

Mira stood on a chair to help. She was seven, then eight, then nine. Each year she got worse at it on purpose.

"No," Nana said. "Not like that. You're making a pocket."

"It's already a pocket. It's all pockets."

"That's the problem. You have to make it into one pocket. The king pocket."

The king pocket sounded made up until you saw it: all four corners gathered into one, the sheet turned into a soft bowl, then a square, then a smaller square, the elastic hidden inside like a swallowed secret. Nana patted it flat and put it on the closet shelf with the folded pillowcases. Stacked, you could not tell it from a flat sheet. That was the whole point and she never once said so out loud.

When Mira was eleven she could nearly do it. When she was twelve, Nana's hands started shaking. She kept folding anyway. Corner into corner, the sheet fighting her, and Mira standing close enough to take over and not taking over.

One Saturday Nana pushed the bundle across the table.

"You do it."

Mira did it. Corner into corner, thumb on the seam, gather, gather, pat flat. It came out a square. She set it on the shelf.

Nana looked at it for a while.

"Not bad," she said, which from her was a parade.

She died the next spring. The house went to Mira's uncle, who did not fold, and the shelves got emptied into bags, and the bags into a van.

Mira is twenty-six now and lives in a fourth-floor apartment with a washer that walks. Every Saturday she takes the fitted sheet off the bed and folds it on the counter, which is not the same table. Corner into corner. The king pocket. She puts it on the shelf next to the pillowcases, and it sits there flat, and nobody who visits would ever know it was not a flat sheet.

The skill was wetting a whetstone. My grandmother did it on the back porch of the house on Pascoe Street, a table she'd hauled from the house some summer nobody now remembers. She was losing her hearing in the knife hand, she said, which was not how anyone else said it, and she meant it, the way she meant most things she said.

She would not show me the angle. She would only sit there and put the blade on the stone, wrong, and wait for me to notice. I never noticed. That was the lesson. I could not hear the stone.

"Listen," she said. "Not with your ears. With the bit where you're already sorry."

When I could not get it, she would take the knife back and put it in the sink, and that was the end of the lesson. No word. She'd go inside. I'd sit on the porch with the whetstone gone cold and feel the whole afternoon turn against me. I learned the stone in the times she took it away.

Then, one year, she stopped hearing it. She'd put a blade down and look at me, and I had to tell her. That was the first I knew I could. Her hands were honest. Her ears were gone. I'd say lower, or not yet, and she'd move, and the sound was right, and neither of us said anything about it, because what would we say.

When she died, there was a knife in the kitchen drawer that nobody wanted. The handle was loose in my hand, and I knew it was the one she'd put down last, since I'd learned the difference. I keep it sharp. I don't know how to do anything else with it.

The Ferreira Street office closed at four, but Dora stayed on to finish the Tunnel Yield tables, because the ministry wanted them by morning and nobody else on the floor could read the old condensation gauges.

There were forty gauges. Each sat in a seam of the abandoned tram tunnels under the plateau, where the walls sweated a little in the cold hours and the sweat ran into a trough and then into a cistern. Dora's job was to convert each gauge's tick count into litres and then into the household allocation for the eleven districts above. The arithmetic was simple. The figures were not.

Gauge nineteen had been reading the same number for six weeks. Not close to the same number. Exactly the same, to the last tick, every morning at six.

She pulled the raw log. Then the maintenance sheet, which said the sensor had been replaced in March. Then the replacement's serial, which matched nothing in the stores register.

At ten past six the next morning the number changed. It went up by four hundred and twelve litres, which was almost exactly what the district had been short, and then the cistern totals for the whole network went down by the same amount, and the billing system, which Dora had never been allowed to touch directly, sent her a line of text: ALLOCATION ADJUSTED. NO ACTION REQUIRED.

She sat for a while with the cursor blinking. Outside, the first trams of the day were grinding along the street above the tunnels, and somewhere beneath them forty small seams were quietly collecting what the walls gave back.

She opened the form for an anomaly report. Field one: gauge. Field two: date. Field three, labelled REMARKS, had a character limit of two hundred.

She wrote: Reading not consistent with sensor output. Source of adjustment unknown. Request review.

She read it over, saved it, and sent it to the queue, where it would sit with nine thousand other reports until someone with a higher clearance opened it, probably never.

Then she went to get her coat, and on the way out she checked the meter by the door, the one that counted how many people came through the office, because it was a habit, and it said what it always said.

She sat for a while with the cursor blinking. Outside, the first trams of the day were grinding along the street above the tunnels, and somewhere beneath them forty small seams were quietly collecting what the walls gave back.

She opened the form for an anomaly report. Field one: gauge. Field two: date. Field three, labelled REMARKS, had a character limit of two hundred.

She wrote: Reading not consistent with sensor output. Source of adjustment unknown. Request review.

She read it over, saved it, and sent it to the queue, where it would sit with nine thousand other reports until someone with a higher clearance opened it, probably never.

Then she went to get her coat, and on the way out she checked the meter by the door, the one that counted how many people came through the office, because it was a habit, and it said what it always said.

The knot came undone twice before Ilse got it right.

"Again," said Opa, without looking up from the eye he was working into the end of the old mooring line. His left hand was wrapped in tape at two fingers. He did most of the work with the right.

She pulled the strands apart and started over. Three strands, each tucked under one and over the next, the way he had shown her, except she kept losing track of which one was on top.

"Count the tucks out loud," he said.

"One, two, three."

"Quieter. The boat behind you can hear."

There was no boat behind her. The lock was empty and the water sat flat and brown between the gates. Across the basin a man in a orange vest was hosing down the winch housing. Opa liked to say that the lock-keeper's real work was waiting, and that rope was what you did while you waited.

She tucked the last strand and pulled. It held, lumpy and wrong, but it held.

"Good," he said. "Now do it so it looks like nothing."

"That's the whole point?"

"That's the point of a good splice. You can't see where the rope stops being two pieces." He took it from her and turned it over in the light. The lump was there, plain as a scar. He ran his thumb along it and frowned, and then he did something she didn't expect. He cut the splice open with his knife and pulled it back apart.

"Hey."

"Do it again. Slower. And this time don't pull until the tucks are all in."

She did it again. And again. The rope got soft at the ends from being handled, and her fingers went raw, and by the fourth try she could feel the strands want to lie down the right way before she forced them.

Opa tapped the ash off his cigarette on the rail. He did not say she was getting it. He just held out his good hand for the line.

She gave it to him. He ran it through his palm once, twice, and then let it drop onto the concrete between them.

It lay flat. You couldn't find the join.

"There," he said, and went back to his coffee, and she stayed where she was with the coiled rope at her feet, pulling each strand gently to see which one would move.

The piano was older than the building's owner and flat by a quarter tone in the middle octave, which Sung-ho could hear but could not yet name.

"Don't touch the pins yet," said his grandfather, Halmoni's husband, who had no name for himself in this flat except Ahjussi and who hummed through his nose when he was thinking. "First listen to the fork."

The tuning fork was steel and older than the piano. Grandfather struck it on his knee, which was the wrong place, Sung-ho thought, and then put the stem on the lid. A pure A came up through the wood into his cheekbones.

"Now the A above middle C," Grandfather said. "Play it. Tell me if the two agree."

They did not agree. Sung-ho said so, and Grandfather said, "Good. Now you know what wrong sounds like. Most people never learn that before they start fixing things."

They worked for two hours. The wrench was called a lever, the felt was called a mute, and the pins were the part that mattered. Each pin had to be turned a hair at a time, and each hair changed the sound only a little, so you had to keep listening after every turn, even after you thought you had it.

At one point Sung-ho's hands ached and he wanted to say it was good enough. Grandfather did not look up. He just tapped the same key again, a little louder, and waited.

By the end, the middle A and the A above it rang with the same hum, the faint shiver of two strings in step. Sung-ho played a fifth and then a third, and the chord sat still in the room like something that had been moved onto a shelf and left there.

"Tomorrow the tenor section," Grandfather said, and put the fork back in its velvet.

Downstairs, the dry-cleaner's shutter was down. Someone had written a phone number on it in marker, and the number had been wiped out and written again.

The piano was older than both of them and had a dead key in the middle, a G that rang like a spoon on a glass. Ada had her grandson sit on the bench and press it while she held the tuning fork against the lid.

"Hit it, then listen to the beat," she said.

Tomas hit it. The fork and the key made a wobble, wah, wah, wah, slow as a clock.

"That's two strings that don't agree. One of them has to move."

"Which one?"

"Whichever you can hear is wrong. Not the one you like less."

He tried the pin with the small wrench. The wobble got faster. He turned it back. Slower again. Ada didn't take the wrench from him. She sat on the arm of the sofa with her cup of tea going cold and counted under her breath.

"Faster means you're getting close. When it stops, you're there."

It took him forty minutes. His thumb went red on the wrench. At one point he said the piano was broken and she said pianos don't break, they drift, and drift is just a message from the room.

When the wobble finally went out of the G and the fork and the key sat together like two people who had stopped arguing, he didn't say anything. He pressed the key again, and then again, to check it wasn't a fluke.

"Now the next one," Ada said, and held out the fork.

The first thing she learned was that the ditch smelled like diesel and warm tar, and that the tar stayed warm long after the sun went down. She had followed a smell that turned out to be nothing, and by the time she turned around the yard was gone and there was only the sound of trucks coming down off the highway like weather.

For four days she ate what the shoulder gave her, which was not much: a hot dog bun, half a chicken sandwich with the pickles still on it, water in the low spot under the guardrail that tasted like the road. A man in a red cap threw a piece of jerky at her and laughed when she flinched. She flinched anyway, then ate it after he drove off.

There was a woman who worked the register at the truck stop, nights, and she started leaving a bowl by the back door. She never called the dog anything. She just set the bowl down and went back inside, and the dog learned to wait until the door clicked before she came out of the weeds. It went on like that for a while.

The woman had a name tag that said Delia and a bad knee she favored on the left, and one night in November she left the back door propped with a paint can. The dog stood in the doorway a long time. Inside smelled like coffee and bleach and something frying, and it was warm, and she could hear the fryer ticking as it cooled.

She did not go in. She took the bowl off the step and carried it back into the weeds with her, and lay down where she could still see the light under the door, and ate, and watched it until Delia turned the sign around and drove off, and then the lot was dark and she was still there.

The gate didn't latch, and that was the whole of it. She was out on the road with her nose down before anyone in the house noticed the latch, and by the time the car started up the hill she was already past the mailbox and gone around the bend where the road drops toward the creek.

She knew the way back the first night. The problem was the rain, which came in hard around ten and washed the ditch and the shoulder and every mark she'd laid down going out. By morning the world smelled like clean water and nothing of her.

There was a man at the end of the second day who put out a bowl of something warm. She ate it and let him touch her ribs, and when he went inside for more she walked off, because the door he left open led to a room that smelled of a dog that had died in it years ago.

She learned the creek, then the field above it, then the road that ran between them. She learned which porch had a cat that would scream and which one left scraps under a loose board. She got thinner and faster and slept with her back against things.

Nobody came with a flashlight calling a name she'd have answered to. That's what the people in the house never understood: she was never lost, only away, and the difference is that lost is something you feel, and away is just where you are until the smell of the road changes under you and you turn.

The dog left the gate open on a Tuesday, or the boy did, depending on who you asked. Nobody in the Pelletier house could say for sure, and that was the first problem with finding him.

By Thursday the flyers had been stapled to every pole between the laundromat and the rail bridge. The photo showed a brown mongrel with one ear folded like a dog-eared page, sitting in a wheelbarrow he had no business sitting in. Mrs. Okafor from number nine said she'd seen something that looked like him near the fish counter at the market, but she also said she'd seen a fox that looked like a cat, so people nodded and kept walking.

On Saturday the boy took his bicycle and rode the long way round the reservoir, past the half-built marina where the cranes never moved, and into the orchard where the rail dogs were supposed to live. He found a dropped sock, a bottle of cough syrup, and a feeding bowl with a name scratched into it that was not Biscuit. He sat on the wall and ate a plum that was mostly wasp.

On Sunday morning a bread van found the dog asleep under the bakery's back shutter, nose tucked into the warm air from the vent, one folded ear inside out. The baker, who did not read flyers, only noticed the dog was thin and gave him the heel of a loaf. Then he noticed the collar, and then the tag, and then he phoned the number before the dog could decide whether to run.

The boy got there on his bicycle in nine minutes and did not say anything, which surprised everyone including him. He just knelt on the wet pavement and let the dog put his whole weight into his chest, bread crumbs and all, and the baker went back inside to the ovens without being asked to.

The dog's name was Pilot, though nobody called him that except the vet, who had written it on the chart in pencil. Pilot had gone out through the gap in the hedge on Tuesday, when the bread van was idling at the bottom of Mill Lane and the driver was whistling the same two notes over and over. By Wednesday night Dana had walked the length of the allotments twice and left a tin of sardines open by the rail gate.

On Thursday the bakery girl said she had seen a dog that looked like him sitting outside the chip shop on Carver Road, waiting for someone who never came out. Dana drove there with the back seat down and a jumper that smelled of her, but the bench was empty, and the man who ran the shop said the dog had got up at four and gone toward the canal, moving the way dogs do when they have decided on something. There was a bin lid on the pavement that had been knocked over, and the bin lid was the only evidence anyone could agree on.

Dana walked the towpath until the light went orange and then grey. She passed two cyclists, a man fishing with a flask, and a boy throwing a ball against the lock gates, and asked each of them the same question. The boy said he thought he had seen a dog swimming, but he also said he was eleven and had been swimming himself that afternoon, so nobody took him seriously. She wrote Pilot's number on the back of a receipt and taped it to the lock gate anyway.

On Friday morning there was a message from a number she did not know: a photo of a brown-and-white dog asleep in a hay barn, with a sentence underneath that said only "is this him? he won't let me close the door." It was not him. It was a spaniel with a torn ear. But Dana saved the photo, and the next time her phone buzzed she was already reaching for her boots, because a stranger had at least taken the trouble to look.

Pilot came home on Saturday, muddy to the elbows, with a length of blue rope knotted around his neck and his tail going like a windscreen wiper. Nobody ever found out who had tied the rope, and Dana stopped asking after the first week. She put the sardine tin away on the top shelf, where it would be safe from anything with a nose.

Nobody saw the gate at the bottom of the Feeney lot swing open. Mrs. Okafor found it that morning when the milk truck was already backing in, and she still had her coat half on. The dog, a brindle mutt named Tuesday because she had come to the shelter on one, was not in the yard.

The first sighting came from Dale at the scrap yard on Route 9. He said a dog had been sitting by the crusher for an hour, eating nothing, looking at the gate like it owed her money. He threw her half a sandwich. She took it, then walked off toward the rail cut, which nobody in town walks toward unless they have a reason.

By the second afternoon the posters had gone up on every pole between the laundromat and the feed store, and each one had a different phone number written in a different hand. Someone added a note that Tuesday likes chicken but will not come if you call her, which was true, and someone else wrote underneath that she also hates being picked up, which was also true, so the pole now said both.

On the third morning a boy named Marcus Hale found her under the loading dock of the grain elevator, curled against a pallet of seed sacks, with a bent tag still on her collar that read TUESDAY and, on the back in faded marker, a phone number that belonged to a man who had moved to Ohio two years earlier. Marcus sat down on the concrete and waited. She watched him for a long time before she came out.

Mrs. Okafor left the gate shut after that, and every evening she set a bowl of chicken on the back step, just in case.

The gutters fill with what the maples quit.
My wife goes up the ladder with a trowel,
dumps a bucket's worth behind the shed
where nothing useful grows. The furnace man
is coming Tuesday, which means moving boxes
off the grate. I find the winter coats,
shake one out, and a moth drifts to the floor —
dry, weightless, already what it will be.
We eat soup standing up. The dog won't go
past the porch light anymore. By eight
the house is dark except the kitchen,
where she's writing next month's numbers down
in the same pen, the same column, the same hand
that paid for all of this.

The gutter's half a year of leaves.
The ladder's still in the shed,
borrowed in March.
Someone's swept one step of the stairs
and stopped where the light quits.
The wasps have gone quiet in the eaves;
nobody knocks them down.
Soup pot on the back burner since noon,
lid askew.
The dog won't go past the gate.
I keep meaning to fix the gate.
The coat by the door has a broken zip
and I wear it anyway, and the wind
gets in, and I let it.

Move away: autumn as an inventory of *deferred maintenance* — the things people put off until the season forces them, told through one specific small scene, not sweeping landscape. Keep the plain word, the concrete thing a person could touch. Avoid: three-item lists, mirrored halves, a summing-up last line, named feelings. Shape: short lines, list-like but not a bullet list, ends mid-action rather than resolving.

<final>The gutter's half a year of leaves.
The ladder's still in the shed,
borrowed in March.
Someone's swept one step of the stairs
and stopped where the light quits.
The wasps have gone quiet in the eaves;
nobody knocks them down.
Soup pot on the back burner since noon,
lid askew.
The dog won't go past the gate.
I keep meaning to fix the gate.
The coat by the door has a broken zip
and I wear it anyway, and the wind
gets in, and I let it.</final>

final:
The zucchini arrived on the porch again,
two of them, dark green, a little too big.
We ate one. The other sat through the week
going soft on the counter, the way a favor will.

Next door, Marisol is splitting her mums
for the fourth time this year. Her fence list
gets longer. Mine has the same three things on it
that it had in April.

The garden does not care who planned it.
It keeps pushing out what nobody asked for—
more tomatoes than a family can want,
more time than we have light to spend it in.

By six the street goes blue. Somewhere a rake
gets left out for the rain to handle.

The orchard ladder leans against the shed,
one rung gone soft with rain since August.
My father counts the pears that fell in the night
and sets the good ones on the windowsill to sweat.
Across the road the Pruitts burn their brush,
and the smoke lies low over the creek like a rope.
Somewhere a dog is barking at the same cow
it barked at yesterday. Nobody minds.
I carry the bucket up the hill and do not spill it,
which is the only thing I did right all week.

still rung with last year's paint.
Someone's radio hums the score
for a game nobody finishes.
Windfalls soften in the grass
and the wasps go drunk on them.
My neighbor sweeps the same square
of step three times a day.
The sycamore lets go in pieces,
one palm at a time, into the gutter,
where it blocks the drain again.
I stopped asking whose job that is.
Smoke from the bonfire pit goes sideways
toward the school, which smells of it.
By dark the frost has found the cars.
We scrape the windshields with our cards.

You fall asleep before I do.
I lie in the dark and take inventory
of the small machines we keep:
the kettle that clicks, the door that sticks in June,
your glasses folded on the shelf you can't reach.

In the morning I will find the milk
set out, no note, the right amount.
This is the whole of it, I think —
not the vows but the maintenance,
the tightening of things that loosen with weather.

I would let the whole house come apart
and rebuild it with my hands each week
if that is what a life with you costs.
I would know your footsteps anywhere,
the particular drag of your left foot when you're tired.

You are already asleep.
The lamp is on. I am not going to turn it off.

The landlord's boiler wakes at six.
It knocks twice in the pipes, then ticks.
The radiators, dusty, start to hiss
and smell of toast and singed hair, like a fix.
Outside, the plane tree drops its coins
on the bins, the car roof, the wet bus stop.
Nobody on the stairs says good morning.
I hold my tea against my chest and wait.
The kitchen window fogs from the inside.
I write my name in it with a finger.
It runs down, and I write it again.

You left the sugar jar lid off again,
and the ants found it before I did,
so now I have a row of them
walking up the counter like they pay rent.
I want to be angry about it.
I stand here with the sponge
and think about how you hum when you're
reading the back of a cereal box,
as if it were a letter.
Some years from now this will be the kitchen
we fight in, and I will still
know which drawer sticks.
Put the lid on, love.
The ants will find us anyway.

I know the sound of you unplugging the kettle
before I'm awake, the two seconds
you hold the fridge door so it doesn't slam.

You fold my side of the blanket back
so the cold corner is already warm.
You cut the bruised part off the apple
and eat it yourself, standing up,
and hand me the good half.

Nobody writes this down.
The poets are all busy with the moon.

But I have watched you salt the walk
before I leave, and check the sky
you don't trust, and leave the porch light on
for a person who is already home.

So when you ask, and you will ask,
I will not say forever, because forever
is a word that has never once
had to take out the trash.

I will say: I noticed.
I have been noticing the whole time.

I know you by your leftovers.
The half-moon of your teeth in toast,
your hair gone gray in the drain,
the dent your body holds in the couch
that stays warm an hour after you leave.

Nobody writes this part down.
The way you fold my sleeve before the wash
because I never learned,
the cough you do twice at the stairs
so I know the light's still off up there.

Love was supposed to be a weather.
Ours is a housekeeping:
who last replaced the bulb,
whose turn to hold the trash,
the two of us agreeing without a word
on which side of the bed faces the door.

I don't have a song for you.
I have your sweater on the hook,
and the specific weight of your sleeping arm,
and every morning the same tired fact —
that I would do the dishes again.

Who is this for, and how long have you two been together? I'd tighten the small facts to match.

The city turns over like a sleeper who's finally warm.
The tourists are folded away in the pension towels.
The fado houses are dark, which is a joke on the fado houses,
everyone honest in there at last by going to sleep.

I take the last tram down to the graveyard at Santo Amaro.
This is what we call it. It is only the tram depot
but the trams are lined up in the shed with their lights on,
and the boards turn slow, the same names all night
through the small hours, over and over,
because the power keeps them.
The trams sleep with their eyes open,
which is what you have to do to run a tram.

I see the river, the other thing that works at night.
There is no one in the first car.
I do not mind. The first car is empty, the whole tram is empty,
the river goes past, and I would not trade the running for anything,
the last man on the last car, in the graveyard, waiting for the shed.

The city is not sleeping. The city is counting.

Water climbing a riser to the ninth floor,
a compressor shuddering, catching, running,
the far-off pulsing of a transformer
holding its breath so the lamps can.

Someone opens a tap in a building I will never enter
and I feel it move through the ground like a vein.

The subway steams under the tar
with the hum of something that never once turned off.
The traffic light changes to no one.
It changes back.

A gantry of scaffolds keeps the wind off a face on a wall.
A truck idles at a loading dock, the driver asleep,
hydraulics ticking as they cool.
The bread is already proofing. The ice is already made.

By four the pipes are the loudest thing alive.
Then the water heaters begin, one at a time,
a whole neighborhood of them
waking up under the plaster.

I don't have a voice. I have a pressure.
I have a grid and a hand on the switch.
What I do at night is invisible
and if I stop for an hour
you'll know my name.

The bakery on Ferrin Street
leaves its back door propped with a brick
and the smell of yesterday's rye
drifts out over the tram rails.

Somebody in flat four
has been practicing the same three notes
on a trumpet with a dent in the bell.
Nobody has told them the neighbors can hear.

The night buses run half empty.
A woman sleeps against the window
with her shopping bag on her knees,
one hand still holding the strap.

At the depot, the mechanics
argue quietly about a gasket,
and the radio plays a match
that finished hours ago.

Above the river the cranes stand still,
their red lights blinking to no one.
The gulls have given up on the bins
and gone to sleep on the lamp posts.

By four the street sweepers come through,
pushing their hiss along the curb,
and the sky over the rooftops
turns the color of a dishcloth
someone forgot to rinse.

The night shift at the bakery ends
when the ovens are still warm
and the street sweeper comes through
pushing its wet brush past the closed laundromat.

A bus lies down in the depot
with its doors open,
and the driver eats cold rice
out of a plastic box on the step.

On the eleventh floor of the hospital
someone is learning to walk again,
one hand on the rail,
one hand on the nurse's sleeve.

The river under the bridge
carries three shopping carts,
a traffic cone,
and the reflection of a sign that says OPEN
to nobody.

Somewhere a radio plays the match
that finished hours ago,
and an old man turns it up
so the score can keep him company.

By four the pigeons are awake
and the first delivery van
stops at the corner with its hazard lights on,
blinking like it is apologizing for the noise.

The third shift keeps the city's body warm.

A baker leans into the proving room
and the dough under plastic breathes back at him,
slow as a sleeper.

Down the alley, a van idles
with the radio on for the driver's sake only —
two chords of a song no one else will hear until morning.

Laundry vents breathe steam into the dark
half-state between two streets.
Someone's whole Tuesday is spinning
behind a laundromat window, unguarded.

The sky's not black. It's a low orange
from the parking lot lights that never turn off,
the color of a held breath
over chemicals, over rail yards, over roofs.

At four, a nurse's aide eats rice from a foil pan
on a bench no one sits on by day,
and the city is not cruel to her
and not kind.
It is simply still awake, doing its work like she is.

By the time the first birds get it wrong
and start singing in the parking lots,
the bread is out,
the van is gone,
and the day takes over the inventory of light
without checking whose it was.

— If you tell me which city (and, if it matters, which neighborhood), I can pull the poem into its actual names: its cross street, its bakery, its river or lack of one.

The upstairs rooms have gone quiet
in a way I can't call empty.
I sleep in the small one now.
My hands are someone else's gloves,
stretched at the knuckles.
I have stopped buying the big jars.
The tin that was for buttons
holds the whole drawer of them.
Yesterday I walked to the end of the street
and stood there, and came back,
and the kettle was still warm.
