The badge worked on the front door and nothing else all morning, which Priya took as a sign that she had not yet been granted any of the rooms she was about to spend her life in. Nadia met her in the lobby holding two coffees and a folder.

"You're the new me," Nadia said, and laughed, and handed her the folder. "Ignore everything in here, they rewrote it wrong."

She was thirty-four and had been at Halvard six years, which she mentioned twice before the elevator. On the fourth floor she walked Priya past the good kitchen to a narrower one with a broken ice machine and showed her which cabinet had the mugs people didn't mind losing, then which cabinet had the good mugs, and said only the second one mattered.

The desk assigned to Priya had a photograph in the top drawer, a family at a beach, none of whom were Priya.

"That's Marcus," Nadia said. "He left. We never cleaned it out. They never clean anything out."

Priya set the photo face down and Nadia turned it back up.

"Leave it," she said. "It's the only honest thing on this floor."

They spent the morning on systems. Nadia taught her the ticketing tool, then the real ticketing tool, then the spreadsheet that existed because the real tool lied. She taught her which requests to answer within the hour and which to let age two days so the requester would solve it themselves, and how to phrase that in the log so it looked like diligence. She taught her the phrase *per my last message*, and when not to use it, and the name of the one director whose emails should be answered in person.

At noon there was a team lunch, catered, held in a conference room named after a mountain. Eleven people introduced themselves and none of them asked Priya anything, which she had been told to expect and had not believed. She sat beside Nadia and ate what Nadia put on her plate.

"You'll get it," Nadia said, watching her watch them. "Six months. You'll know where everyone is weak."

In the afternoon Nadia took her to the roof, which was locked to everyone but not to Nadia, because Nadia had asked once, years ago, and the facilities manager had never said no.

"I'm leaving in six weeks," she said. She said it looking at the parking deck, not at Priya. "They don't know I know. This is the replacement post — they always fill it first."

Priya started to say something out of the shape of condolence, and Nadia waved it off.

"Don't. It's good. I wanted it." She drank the last of the morning coffee, which she had been carrying around all day. "The reason I'm telling you is that nobody told me. I spent my first day being taught to love this place, and my last year being taught what it cost. I'd rather you got both." She finally looked over. "So. Ask me the thing you'll otherwise figure out at month eight."

Priya thought about the mug cabinet. About the photo left face up. About eleven people who hadn't asked her a single question.

"Why are you telling me the truth on my first day?" she said. "You don't know me."

Nadia nodded like the question had been on the list. "Because I'm going to be gone," she said, "and you're going to be here, and somebody should tell the truth at least once per handover, or it just keeps going." She pushed off the wall. "Come on. I'll show you how to book the room nobody can book."

At five the office emptied in a smooth orderly way. Priya took the elevator down with the badge that opened nothing but the front door, and outside the light was the flat gold of a Tuesday in a city that did not know or care that she had started a job that day. She stood on the sidewalk with the folder full of wrong instructions.

She called her sister.

"It went fine," she said. "I met one person."

The badge said NADIA, though nobody had asked for her name yet. She stood at the loading bay door of the cold-storage depot with her lunch in a tote bag and watched a forklift reverse past her without slowing down.

Inside, a woman with a clipboard was counting crates of frozen peas, saying each number under her breath like a rosary. "You're the new one," she said, not looking up. "Agnieszka. Four hundred and twelve. Four hundred and thirteen. Don't touch the blue pallets, they're mine."

The induction was a laminated sheet and a man named Tomasz who had been there nineteen years and spoke only about the freezer door, which had to be lifted and pushed at the same moment or it stuck. He showed her twice. The third time she did it alone and it gave with a crack like a knuckle, and he nodded once and went back to his tea.

At eleven the power to the east aisle dropped for a minute and every light went amber. Nobody panicked. Agnieszka kept counting. Someone shouted "back up" from the dark, and then the lights came on again, and the forklift was still there, a yard from where she had been standing.

At lunch she sat on an upturned crate by the bay door. Tomasz came out with his tea and sat on the next crate without a word. After a while he said, "The door sticks for everyone the first week. Second week it sticks for you only when you're tired."

She ate her sandwich. Outside, a delivery van idled with its engine on, and a dog barked somewhere past the fence.

At four she found her locker, which had a sticker of a cartoon fish on the inside door that someone had peeled half off. She left it that way.

The badge had her photo from the interview, which was taken in the wrong light. Nobody had told her that the badge reader by the side door sticks on the first swipe, so she stood there for a while, waving her card at a red light, until a man from receiving leaned out of a loading bay and said, "Lift it, then push." She lifted it, then pushed. It opened.

Inside, the building smelled of toner and the cold coffee from the machine that nobody cleaned. Her desk was in a row of four, between a plant that was clearly dead and a stack of unopened boxes labeled in her manager's handwriting: SAMPLES, DO NOT, and then nothing, the marker had run out.

Her manager showed her where the printer was and where the good stapler lived. She did not show her where the bathroom key was, because there was no key, only a rule that you did not use the second floor one after two o'clock.

At eleven someone asked if she wanted to join the lunch order. She said yes without knowing what it was. It was four sandwiches, one of which was hers, and a bag of crisps that everyone pretended to share fairly.

In the afternoon she was given a login, a folder of files with names that did not match their contents, and one task: find out why the Thursday report had two columns that said the same thing. She opened the first file. Then she opened the second. Around four she found the cause, a formula someone had copied down a row too far in another year, and she sat back and looked at it for a while, the only thing that day that she was sure of.

At five the lights on her floor went off in sections, one row at a time, and she stayed in the last lit row, still in her coat, until the sensor gave up on her too.

Marisol had been told to arrive at eight, so she was in the lobby at seven-forty, holding a visitor badge that someone had already printed with the wrong spelling of her surname. A man at the security desk noticed her looking at it and shrugged. "They print them in batches. Yours is the Tuesday batch."

Her manager, Teodor, came down at eight-fifteen with a coffee in each hand and gave her one without asking how she took it. It was already milky. She drank it anyway.

The floor was loud with keyboards and a printer that jammed twice before nine. Nobody was introduced to her formally. She learned names by overhearing them: Priyanka, who ran the shared calendar and was furious about it; Dov, who answered every question with a question; a woman called Hsu-Ling who kept a jar of clothespins on her desk and clipped one to her cardigan whenever she stood up, so the cardigan had a dozen of them by eleven.

At ten, Teodor gave her a laptop that had someone else's stickers still on the lid. She had a login and a folder called "onboarding" that was empty except for a file named "READ ME FIRST" that was a blank document.

She asked Dov what the blank file was for. He thought about it. "Teodor writes it at the end of the week," he said. "Usually it's about the printer."

At lunch she sat alone by the window. Across the street a bakery was closing its shutters. She ate a sandwich she had made at six in the morning and wondered whether anyone would notice she hadn't gone to the cafeteria.

Hsu-Ling came over and sat down with a tray of noodles. "First day," she said. It wasn't a question. Marisol nodded. Hsu-Ling took a clothespin off her cardigan and clipped it to the edge of Marisol's notebook without comment, then went back to her noodles.

In the afternoon she was given a real task: reconcile two spreadsheets that disagreed by four hundred and twelve dollars. She found the cause at four-thirty. A supplier had been entered twice, once with a trailing space in the name. She fixed it and sent a message to Teodor. He replied in under a minute: "Good. Now go home. Tomorrow the printer will be worse."

On the way out she passed the security desk. The man there said, "How was it?"

"The printer is worse," she said.

He laughed, and she realized she had been holding the badge the whole day, and she handed it back to him, and he put it in a bin with a hundred others.

Marguerite Osei was at her desk when I arrived, and nobody had told her I was coming, or nobody had told me she hadn't gone.

The badge printer in the basement had my name but not my photo. It showed a gray silhouette where my face should be, and the woman at the machine said this happens when HR opens the file before the hire date, and to come back Thursday. I clipped it on anyway. Walking down the fourth-floor hall with a gray head hanging over my chest, I practiced the name of the man I was replacing, because I had said it forty times in interviews and had never once pictured the person attached to it.

His office was the third door. There were two chairs. She was in one, and her coat was still on the back of the other.

"You're the new one," she said.

"Yes."

"They said January."

"It's January."

She looked at the calendar on the wall, which was also still December, and something in her face closed like a drawer. She was maybe sixty. She had a cardigan the color of oatmeal and a mug with a name on it that wasn't hers—Gary, in blue letters—and I understood that Gary had been here before both of us and that the mug outlasted him too.

She showed me where the coffee was. She showed me which drawer stuck. She did not show me the files, or the system, or the thing she had been doing in that chair for nineteen years, and I did not ask, because it was nine in the morning and the floor was quiet and two people were in one office and there was only one name on the door.

At eleven a man stopped in the hall and said "Marguerite, you're back," and she said "I'm still here," and he laughed and walked on, and she looked at me the way you look at weather coming in.

I organized the supply closet to have something to do. I alphabetized things that were already alphabetized. At noon I ate a sandwich in the break room while a woman named Deb told me about her son's knee surgery and asked nothing about me, which was a kindness, or felt like one.

At two Marguerite came to the doorway with her coat. She had her bag. She said my name correctly, which no one else had managed, and then she said: "The password's the same as the username. They'll change it Monday. It hasn't changed since 2009." And she left, and her mug stayed on the desk, Gary's mug, and I did not move it.

The system let me in. The screen was full of her work—dates in a column, a font from another era, initials in the corner of every file: M.O., M.O., M.O., down the page like footprints. I read a few. I didn't change anything.

At five the lights came down in rows. I put on my coat with the gray face swinging under it, and turned off her lamp, and stood in the door for a second not sure what I was supposed to do with the mug, and left it where it was. On the way out I passed Deb, who said see you tomorrow, and I said see you tomorrow, and heard myself say it in her voice, the room's voice, the floor's—flat, kind, used. On the train home I caught the badge in the window glass. Gray face, real name. Both of them true.

Coming in on the night ferry, the deck lights
cut a path we could not see the end of,
and my father, who had been down to the water
his whole life, said nothing about the water.

He counted the bell buoys. One. Two. One.
He knew what was under us, the way a man
knows the back of his own hand, its four
small scars. He brought back what he took out

and threw back the rest, and if a tide
gave him nothing, he said nothing, which passed
for praise. I want to say something true
about the surface. I have never seen it.

The tide goes out and leaves its bill.
The men come down with a bucket and a hook.
They are not looking at the water.
They are looking at the bolts, the tarred rope,
whether the fender held.

Nobody here writes about the sea.
They write about Tuesday, when the pump went.
The salt gets into everything that earns.
The gulls are just birds that are good at their job.

At dusk the light comes flat off the harbor
and the ones still working do not look up.
The ocean is a thing you keep out of the cabin.
It is also the thing that pays.

If you stand here long enough you learn
it never once asked to be beautiful.

Marguerite had been at the front desk of Halvorsen & Pike for nineteen years, long enough to know that new people arrive wearing their good shoes and holding their coats too carefully, as if the coats might be asked to leave.

The man this morning was called Tobias Ream. He had a lanyard already, which meant someone had remembered him, which was more than usual. He stood in the lobby and read the framed photographs on the wall, the way they all did, looking for a face that would tell him what kind of place he had walked into.

"Second floor," she said. "Lift's temperamental. Take the stairs if you want to be on time."

"Thank you." He hesitated. "Is it always this quiet?"

"Only before nine. After that Gerald starts shouting about the coffee."

He laughed, a little too loudly, the way they did when they had decided to be pleasant before they were sure they were allowed to be.

She watched him go up the stairs. Two steps at a time, then one, then two again. Fine. He would find his desk, and someone would show him where the stapler lived, and by eleven he would have stopped apologising for existing in the room.

Nineteen years. The first day was always the same and never the same. The people who stayed were rarely the ones who were brilliant on day one. They were the ones who asked where the good sandwiches were, who remembered her grandson's name on the second visit, who did not pretend to know what the acronyms meant.

At half past ten he came back down, pretending to look for something in his bag.

"Found it?" she asked.

"Found a pen," he said. "Which is more than I expected."

"There's a drawer for pens. Top left, under the calendar. Everybody loses one in the first week."

He looked at her properly then, as if she had just told him something useful and not just a fact about stationery. "Thanks," he said. "Really."

"Don't thank me yet. Wait until Gerald's coffee."

He went back up. She did not watch this time. She had a phone to answer, and a pile of post, and somewhere on the second floor a stranger was learning the shape of a place that would, in a month or two, feel like it had always been his.

**The Loss Adjuster Explains Why the Sea Is Not Insured**

Salt lies about everything.
It writes on brass the way a doctor writes,
illegibly and late. I come after,
with my camera and my flashlight and my forms,
to say how much of this was the wind
and how much was the boat, and how much
was a man who didn't want to go home.

I have stood on the Orkney pier at four a.m.
with a thermos and a clipboard and decided, formally,
that the ocean owes no one anything,
and watched the widow take it the way you take
a bill you already paid.

The surveyors say the seabed's like a quilt
of quilted coal. The echo comes back wrong
off mud. So they drop lead on a line,
still, the old way, grease on the base,
and read what sticks: sand, shells, shale.
You know the sea by what it lets itself be touched by.

Last week, a phone. A yacht, three weeks out.
Water in the fuel. Not weather, I said.
The sea doesn't steal. It simply keeps
whatever you were holding
when you stopped holding it.

I put down: *recovered, two. Not recovered, one.*

Offshore, past the file, the swells go on
doing the long arithmetic.
Nothing at sea is missing.
There is no lost.
Only a count of what is elsewhere now,

and the forms, drying,
and the sea not owing.

The sea is not a metaphor at this address.
It is a wet neighbor that never sleeps,
that drags its nails along the seawall
all night and leaves a rind of salt
on everything I own.

My hinges know it. My car knows it.
The third step down to the beach knows it,
worn to a slick gray tongue by boots
that keep going down and coming back
with sand in the cuffs and nothing to show.

It takes things on a schedule no one printed.
A ring. A dog, once. The good knife.
It gives back a boot two towns over
six weeks later, and a message in a bottle
that turns out to be someone's grocery list.

I have stopped calling it beautiful.
Beautiful is for guests.
I call it the thing that ate my July,
that rusts the chain, that will not be reasoned with,
that I keep walking toward anyway,
every morning, with the dog,
past the broken pier,

and I do not know why, exactly,
except that it is always there,
and it is always leaving,
and there is a sound it makes
when it goes out
that is the only quiet
I have ever trusted.

The badge said HOLLOWAY, R., and the photo was from eleven years ago, when Rhian had still worn her hair short and believed in lanyards.

Nobody had told her the lift was slow on the left. She pressed the button three times, then took the stairs with the box of her things against her hip, a mug, a cactus wrapped in a receipt, a paperback she had not meant to bring. The fourth floor smelled of toner and oranges.

"You'll be Rhian," said a man at a desk by the window. He had a cardigan the colour of weak tea and a biro behind each ear. "Desk's the one with the good drawer. Locker key's on the hook. Don't lose it, Pauline will want it back in person."

"Pauline?"

"Pauline is everyone's manager and nobody's friend." He said it kindly. "Tea rota's on the fridge. You're Thursday. Don't be Thursday at ten past, because Ajay does Thursday and he takes it personally."

She put the cactus on the windowsill. The receipt was from a garden centre in a town she had lived in for two years and never once thought of as home. She folded it into the drawer with the good pens.

At half ten someone left a mug of tea on her desk without a word. It was too sweet and exactly right. She didn't ask who. She drank it anyway, looking at the badge on its clip, the photo of a woman who had been braver.

At twelve the window office emptied for lunch and the room got quiet enough to hear the radiator tick. Rhian opened the paperback to the page she had marked, then closed it again, because she had not come here to be a person reading in a corner.

At four the man in the cardigan came back and set a second mug down beside the first.

"Earl Grey," he said. "Don't tell Ajay."

She laughed, which surprised her, and the laugh went down the room and came back up as someone else's.

On the way out she stood at the locker and turned the key over. It was warm from her hand. She fitted it into the lock, and it turned easily, and that was the whole of it: a small thing that worked the first time, which she decided to count.

The lift was still slow on the left. She took the stairs.

**Chart of an Unnamed Body**

We know it by the road that turns
to face it and then gives up.

By the salt that gets into the hinges,
by the paint that leaves the railing first.

By the gulls that have learned
the schedule of the trawlers better than we have.

By the lighthouse, which is a way of saying
we do not trust it after dark.

Somewhere under the shipping lanes
the cables lie like a second coastline,
voices in glass, a whole century's gossip
running along the floor.

The pilot whales go over the shelf
without a sound we can hear.
The sonar counts them anyway.

On the cliff the woman keeps a lamp
she does not light. She says the dark
is the only map that has never lied.

At low tide the children are allowed
to go as far as the marker post.
Beyond it, the ground becomes a rumor.

My sister sends me a shell she found,
wrapped in a page of a phone book.
On the phone I say I'll put it to my ear,
but I put it to my knee, to my cheek,
to the small of my back,
which is not where you hear things.
It is where you hold something cold
you don't want to put down.

The ocean is a neighbor I have never spoken to,
though every night it walks its dog
against my wall. I know its hours.
I know it rearranges the mail.
I know it takes back what it lends:
the dog, the wall, the argument.
Somewhere a woman I have never met
is standing in it to her waist
and it is not holding her,
it is choosing not to take her yet.
That is the part she tells no one,
how close those are, how warm the choice.

I hang the shell on a nail by the door,
where a coat would go, if a coat were ever cold enough.
It is a house, the shell. It is a room
where the ocean kept its one small noise
so it could find its way back to itself,
so it could always be walking up my stairs.
I lock the plain door. It does not care.
I am inside its weather and it is inside mine
and we do not exchange a word
and that is the whole arrangement.

The sea keeps a lost-property office.
Nobody goes there on purpose.

It has a left shoe, green with weed,
still laced, still tied in a double knot.

sorts the shelf again.

Nothing gets claimed.

in the wrong town, weeks later,
to a woman walking a dog
who picks up the glove
and does not know why she is crying.

The tide is a clerk who never sleeps.
Each dawn she comes in with her cart of wet paper
and writes the shoreline out again,
a little to the left of yesterday's.

She keeps the forms for everything:
the shell's pale signature,
the gull's three neat prints,
the child's castle, filed under Lost.

By noon the sun has read every page.
By dusk she is taking the drafts back,
folding the kelp into soft carbon,
pressing the sand flat as a ledger.

No one has ever seen her finish.
The light comes down the hall of the bay,
and somewhere a drawer she has not opened
keeps the whole sea, unsigned.

The sea does not keep accounts.
It takes the anchor, the bottle,
the name scratched into a bench at the pier,
and does not ask what they meant.

Here is a ring that slipped from a hand
in a cold year nobody remembers.

a letter folded twice and never sent.

smoothed and softened,
laid along the sand like gifts
no one is sure they were meant to receive.

We walk the wet line in the morning
and pick up what we can carry.
The water watches, patient,
keeping the rest.

The badge had her name on it, spelled right, which Mara took as a good sign until she noticed the photo was from someone else's ID card and had been cropped to fit.

"Don't mind that," said the man at the desk, who gave his name as Ferris and did not look up for long. "Facilities made them in a batch. Yours was the last one left."

He handed her a clipboard. On it was a floor plan of the third floor, every room numbered, and a column of tick-boxes headed STATUS.

"Inventory," he said. "Desks, chairs, phones, what's still plugged in. Anything with a label goes on the list. Anything without a label goes in the bin by the stairs."

The third floor was almost empty. Long fluorescent tubes buzzed over rows of desks with nothing on them but a mug, a stapler, a single shoe. She checked the first box and wrote *desk 14, chair, phone (dead)*. The chair still had a sticky note on its back: *Ask Dev about the Thursday numbers.*

She did not ask Dev. Dev had left in March, according to the HR email, and so had most of the people whose desks she passed.

By eleven she had a rhythm. Desk, chair, label, tick. Desk, chair, label, tick. Once she found a child's drawing of a horse taped under a monitor, the horse wearing a party hat. She stood with it for a while, then wrote *drawing (personal) — return?* in the margin and put it gently into a folder marked UNSURE.

At lunch she went down to the cafeteria, which had three tables still set up and a woman behind the counter with a name tag reading ROSALIND, GROUNDS.

"First day?" Rosalind asked, filling a paper cup with coffee that tasted of the machine.

"Second. I think. Yesterday was orientation, but they didn't show me this floor."

"Nobody shows you this floor." Rosalind slid a biscuit across the counter. "You're counting what's left."

"Yes."

"Good. Somebody should." She nodded toward the window, where the parking lot was half empty. "You'll be surprised how many people want to know their coffee mug got collected. They ask. They never come back for it, but they ask."

Mara went back up at one o'clock with the biscuit in her coat pocket and a strange lightness in her chest. The work was not hard. It was only slow and sad and very precise, and nobody had asked her to be cheerful about it.

At four she reached room 31, the corner office, its door standing open. On the desk was a framed photo of a lighthouse and a cardboard box half full of pens. She checked the box. She wrote *pens (assorted), 22*. Then she stood in the doorway a moment longer than the job required, looking out at the grey lot and the lit windows of the building across the road, where, she supposed, someone else was also starting something new.

At five Ferris came by with a fresh clipboard and a rubber stamp.

"Done?"

"Almost. The third floor's clear except for the horse."

He looked at the folder marked UNSURE and nodded. "Keep it. Put it on your desk tomorrow. Somebody will come asking."

He stamped the top sheet. The ink said COMPLETE in capital letters, and under it, in smaller letters someone had clearly added by hand, *first day*.

She took the badge off, read her name once more, and clipped it to her coat.

THE DRAWER.

Everyone has one. Second drawer down, left of the stove. Inside: forty rubber bands, three dead batteries, a takeout menu from a place that closed, a birthday candle, one screw.

Here is what no one tells you about that drawer.

Rubber bands do not last forever. They dry. They go brittle. In the dark, over years, they slump into the wood grain and stay there — a soft black line you can't scrub out, shaped like the band that made it. The drawer keeps a record of everything you meant to use.

This is not a drawer problem. This is a you problem. You put things there because you couldn't decide about them.

We make a small tin box. It has a lid. It costs less than the takeout you never ordered from that menu. You put the rubber bands in the tin. The tin goes in the drawer. The drawer stops keeping records.

The batteries still go to the recycling center. We can't help you with the candle.

TIN. One drawer, one lid.

Everything we let go of
went somewhere down there.

The wedding ring, the first tooth,
a key to a house that was pulled down
before anyone in this town could drive.
The letter that was never sent
is still folded, still damp, still
waiting for a reader who has not yet
learned to swim.

The ocean keeps its own inventory.
It does not sort. It does not ask
why the sandal was lost or whose name
was scratched into the spoon.
It holds the spoon the way
a patient clerk holds a filing cabinet
no one has opened in a century.

Sometimes a wave gives something back:
a bottle with no message, a shoe
with a foot still somehow inside,
a shell that sounds like the room
it was taken from.

Most nights the tide keeps the archive closed.
Stand at the edge and you are only
the most recent thing it has been handed.

Sold in pairs because you have two.

**WEDGE**

*The doorstop.*

You did not choose it. It came with the flat, or your father had one in the garage, or it fell out of a wall in 1994 and stayed.

Here is what it has been doing since.

It has held the door while you carried groceries in with both arms. It has held the door while the cat decided, slowly, whether to come back inside. It has held the door during the argument you had in the hallway, when the only thing keeping the two of you from walking out was that someone had to step over the wedge.

No battery. No app. No firmware update that moves the button.

It does one thing: it stops the door from being the door that closes.

Slip it under. Walk away. Come back to a room that is still open.

Fixed: 5 ideas, numbered, two sentences each, startup-format for underserved market. Default: generic apps for seniors, rural telehealth, immigrants, disabled people, low-income. Directions: (1) material — workers compensation clinics and claims paperwork; (2) lens — teenagers who are primary translators for their families in emergency rooms; (3) subtraction — remove the smartphone/consumer assumption from recovery services. 1. A payroll-recovery tool for home care workers who are paid by the visit, not the hour, and routinely lost time between appointments. It reconstructs unpaid travel and wait time from calendars and call logs, then files the wage claim with the state labor office.

2. A translation layer for teenagers who interpret for their families in hospitals, emergency rooms, and school meetings. It prepares the teen before a visit with the medical or legal terms they will need to say, then coaches them out of the role when an adult interpreter should be called.

3. A benefits-verification service for small landlords who rent to tenants with housing vouchers. It pre-checks inspection paperwork, tracks the agency’s response, and gives the landlord a calendar that only includes the deadlines they cannot miss.

4. A shipping and returns service for the rural last-mile sellers of livestock, produce, and handmade goods. It pools boxes across nearby sellers, prints the one label each county’s only carrier actually accepts, and handles the pickup window.

5. A training and equipment marketplace for the adult children who suddenly become unpaid caregivers for a parent. It teaches one specific task at a time, like giving a shot or lifting someone from a bed, and rents the equipment for exactly that week.

If this reads more like a list of services than software companies, that is the point: the underserved part of these markets is usually the paperwork, not the app.
</final>

3. 4. A letting service for hallways, side rooms and disused canteens that schools, churches and clubs hold but never book out. It lists only spaces under 40 seats, because the big platforms price and filter in a way that buries them.

5. A kit and guide for turning out a first hot meal under real pressure — a broken gas line, a flooded kitchen, a town where the shops shut — written for people who can cook nothing yet. Sold as a folded card and a pantry list, not an app.

One question, so these land closer to your case: which of the five is nearest to something you already know from the inside?

final: The empire has no wizards, only archivists. For three hundred years the Mandate of Heaven — the signature that proves an emperor is chosen — has been forged, repaired and re-dated by a guild of clerks who keep the single page in a humidity-controlled vault and have never once let it be examined by sunlight. Their newest apprentice, hired for her handwriting, notices that the signature is getting fresher: the ink is supposed to be nine generations old and it is about eleven years old. Then the sitting emperor announces he will display the Mandate in public for the first time, and the guild has six weeks to make a forgery that can survive being looked at by a hundred thousand people, one of whom may be the last person alive who watched the original being written.

1. **Tool-lending co-op for renters.** Many people in dense cities own a drill, a ladder, or a pressure washer they use twice a year, while renters with no storage pay for each one. A building-level lending library, run through the building's existing mailing and access systems, would turn idle equipment into shared capacity.

2. **Scheduling software for home-based hair braiders.** Independent braiders, many of them Black women running businesses from kitchens and spare rooms, often manage bookings through text threads and paper calendars that lose deposits and double-book clients. A booking tool built around their deposit rules, style-length pricing, and rebooking habits would fit how they already work.

3. **Pharmacy-adjacent medication pickup for rural seniors.** Elderly patients in small towns often cannot reliably drive to a pharmacy, and missed refills lead to hospital visits that cost far more. A service that bundles prescription pickup with a regular, scheduled delivery route run by local drivers would close that gap.

4. **Interpreter booking for small clinics and trades.** Independent clinics, dental offices, and contractors serving limited-English communities usually cannot afford a full-time interpreter but still face frequent language barriers. An on-demand marketplace of vetted, part-time medical and trade interpreters, billed by the minute, would give them access without a staffing contract.

5. **Repair-first resale for used baby gear.** Parents buy car seats, strollers, and cribs secondhand, but many items have expired, been recalled, or are missing parts, and sellers rarely check. A marketplace that verifies recall status, expiration dates, and completeness before listing, with a simple inspection badge, would make secondhand baby gear safer to buy.

A coastal city where the sea is slowly rising, and the only thing that holds it back is a guild of divers who swim down and physically tie the tide to the harbor floor with knotted rope — every high tide, every day, by hand. The knots hold because the divers die holding them, and the city has a waiting list for the job that is longer than the wait for a grave. The story follows the clerk who keeps that list: she assigns people to drown, and she has started quietly moving names up and down it for reasons that are not on the form, which works fine until the drowned start keeping records too.

What's the one thing you'd want this to be about — grief, or the bureaucracy itself?

The business sells repair time and a reason to come back, to households and retirees who throw away working machines because no one nearby will fix them.

2. **Shift-work childcare scheduler for hospital and warehouse staff:** A booking platform that matches nurses, warehouse workers and other odd-hour employees with vetted sitters who work exactly the overnight, split and weekend blocks their rosters create. Employers pay a subsidy per shift, which reduces absenteeism and gives workers a benefit that standard daycare hours never cover.

3. **Dialect-first voice assistant for older rural speakers:** A voice interface trained on regional accents and local place names, with a simple phone-call setup that needs no smartphone or app store account. It targets residents in areas where mainstream assistants misunderstand speech, which leaves them without tools for medication reminders, transport bookings and calling family.

4. **Subscription sourcing service for small-batch food producers:** A marketplace that buys surplus ingredients from small farms and bakeries that sell too little to qualify for wholesale distributors, then ships them in standing weekly orders. Producers gain predictable buyers and a fixed price, while the platform takes a margin on the consolidated volume they could never negotiate alone.

5. **Pre-trial paperwork assistant for self-represented tenants:** A guided tool that walks renters through eviction notices, deadlines and court forms in plain language, and connects them to a volunteer law clinic when a case needs a lawyer. Most evictions are decided against tenants who never filed a response, so the product aims at the single missing step that decides the outcome.

final: The miller's daughter in Tirre can scrape the dye off any thread with her thumbnail, which is why the town's tally clerk keeps her ledger in a locked drawer and why the duke's steward rides eleven days to buy her — not for the magic, but because the province's winter wool levy has to come out of the weavers somehow, and a woman who can read a dishonest thread is cheaper than a war. She goes, since the alternative is her mother's rent, and finds the duke is not dying heroically but stalling: he owes the crown a debt written in cloth that will not hold its color, and someone upstream has been quietly stretching it thinner each year. She keeps the colors honest because that is the work, and because the people who depend on the weave are the ones who will freeze if it fails, and by the time she understands that untangling the fraud will ruin every weaver whose name is signed to it, she has already signed her own.

final: In the drowned city of Corr, where the tide has taken the lower districts and the river now runs over the rooftops, the ferry-women are the only ones who still know which streets lead anywhere. When the eldest of them, Iselde Marr, dies with a debt unpaid to the eel-merchants, her apprentice Tam inherits both her boat and her ledger of favors owed. The ledger is written in a private shorthand, and one entry names a man who has been dead for forty years and still sends letters. Tam sets out to collect on it, through flooded archives, a guild of bell-ringers who measure the water by sound, and a bridge that rebuilds itself each night. What she finds is that the city was never sinking. It was being quietly rowed somewhere, one debt at a time, and the person steering it is someone who has been paying in her own name.

1. **Compliance-in-a-box for small freight brokerages.** New brokers drown in carrier vetting paperwork, and most quit or get fined before their first profitable lane. A service that runs vetting, insurance certificate tracking, and audit prep for a flat monthly fee sells certainty to people who can't afford a compliance hire.

2. **Replacement-parts concierge for independent appliance repair techs.** These techs lose jobs waiting on hold with manufacturers and guessing which of six near-identical parts fits. A single lookup-and-order desk, charged per part, turns their dead time into billable calls.

3. **Scheduling and billing built for mobile phlebotomy.** Drawing blood at people's homes means routes, temperature-sensitive samples, and insurers who pay weeks late. A tool that plans the route, logs the cold chain, and chases the claim hits three pains nobody's software addresses together.

4. **Dead-stock exchange for church and school supply closets.** Every parish and district has shelves of unused curriculum, chairs, and choir robes, and no way to find the parish three towns over that needs exactly that. A barter-and-sale marketplace with denominational and district filters turns hoarding into a budget line.

5. **Night-shift childcare for hospital and warehouse workers.** Standard daycare hours match nobody who clocks in at 7 p.m. A licensed overnight site near the industrial park, billing by the shift, serves parents every other provider has quietly written off.

final:
Marta Okonkwo restores player piano rolls. Not the pianos — the rolls, the perforated paper that tells the machine which keys to press. She works in a converted garage in a town where the mill closed and nobody updated the sign. Her hands are steady and her hearing is going: forty years of sitting inside a mechanical piano's guts while it plays has left her right ear mostly dead and her left ear tuned to a narrow band — the clack of a pneumatic valve, the hiss of a leak, the exact moment a roll's paper has stretched past what the tracker bar can read.

This is how she notices things. Not faces. Not lies. She notices what a person's hands did. A roll is a record of somebody's touch: how hard they leaned into a key, how long they held it, where they hesitated because the arrangement was hard or because they were tired or because they were thinking about something else entirely. She has spent her life reading strangers' hands through holes in paper, decades after the hands are gone.

So when a man turns up dead in the boarding house two streets over, and the sheriff — who knew Marta's husband before he died, who still calls her Mrs. Okonkwo like it's a rank — brings her a roll found in the dead man's room, she does the thing she actually knows how to do. She reads it.

The roll is labeled with a tune she's never heard of, which means nothing; people relabel things. But it was punched by hand, not cut by a factory machine, and the punchwork is a signature as good as a name. The right hand plays with the flat, even pressure of someone who practiced. The left hand is all over the place — rushing, dragging, catching up — like the person punching it was being watched and didn't want to be, or was in a hurry to be done with something they also wanted to get right.

Marta doesn't solve the murder by asking questions. She can't. Her version of an interrogation is a room full of silence and a roll of paper going around a spool, and what she gets out of it is that the person who made it was left-handed in a way that fights against the way the paper feeds, and that they punched three bars twice in a row by mistake — the same mistake twice, which means they weren't copying a tune from memory. They were copying from a source. Somewhere in this town is another roll, and whoever owns it also owns the shape of the dead man's last evening.

She isn't brave. She's seventy-one and her knees hurt and she has no interest in being a hero. What she has is a specific, useless-seeming skill and a growing certainty that the person who punched this roll knows she's the only one in town who could read it. That makes her, for reasons she finds personally inconvenient, the only person the killer needs to talk to.

Wren Kaluža has read six hundred burned buildings and has never once been asked what she thought.

She works for a mid-sized insurer, the kind that insures laundromats, car washes, and the four-unit walk-ups nobody photographs. When a building burns, she arrives before the fire marshal has taped the door, wearing boots and a clipboard that no longer holds paper. Her job is to price the loss. Her actual skill is that she can walk a gutted room and tell you where the fire started, which way it moved, and roughly how long the room stood before anyone called it in — from the shape of the char at the baseboard, the sag of a steel joist, the pattern of glass on the sidewalk.

But that is not the unusual part. The unusual part is what she does with a building that burned for a reason nobody has said out loud.

She keeps a second set of files. Not the official ones — those list square footage and replacement value and go to a claims desk in another state. Her set lists what the room was doing when it caught: the chair pulled to the window, the two coffee cups on the sill, the padlock on a door that had no exterior key. She photographs these too, separately. She has never shown them to anyone. She is not sure yet what they're for.

The mystery starts with the Faro Street job: a laundromat fire, ruled accidental, wiring in the wall. And in Wren's photographs, the same six things are wrong that were wrong in two other laundromats that burned in the last fourteen months, in three different towns. Same missing coin box. Same row of dryers moved two feet from the wall. She knows what that pattern means. She has seen it in a hundred honest fires: someone rearranged the room first.

She has no badge, no gun, and no standing to say a word. What she has is a legitimate reason to be inside the building before anyone else, and a boss who thinks she spends too long on site because she's thorough. She will spend the next two hundred pages doing the one thing she is qualified to do and pretending it is something else.

**Name:** Ilse Marrow-Vance, 61, a retired ferry timetable compiler who now works nights repairing hearing aids in a shop above a launderette.

**The unusual part:** She cannot tell when people are lying, but she can always tell when a clock has been moved. Thirty-one years of reconciling departure boards left her with an ear for minutes that are slightly wrong. She notices a bus that is four minutes early because someone wanted it to be, and she notices a wristwatch that was reset after a death.

**Her method:** She does not interview suspects. She asks them what time they had their last meal, what time the kettle went on, and what the radio was playing. People answer without thinking, and their answers rarely agree with each other.

**Her flaw:** She trusts timetables more than people, and she has never once checked whether the timetables were honest. Her own husband's disappearance in 1994 was logged as a 7:12 departure that she compiled herself. She has never reopened it.

**The case that finds her:** A hearing-aid customer, a man she has seen on the 7:12 every weekday for two years, comes in with a device that no longer picks up the chime of the station clock. He says he cannot hear the time anymore. Ilse notices that the chime he describes is one that was switched off during a refit eleven years ago.

**Why she is unusual:** She is a mystery protagonist who solves by listening to the wrong detail in an ordinary routine, and whose own unsolved loss is hidden inside the very schedule she spent her career perfecting.

Alma Reyes has rekeyed most of the doors in Marrow Creek. She is nineteen and keeps the shop's master ledger in a spiral notebook she bought herself, because her uncle's system is a shoebox.

The notebook has a column for the address, a column for the lock, and a column she calls *tell* — what a person's keyring says about them. The florist keeps four copies of the back door key and none of the front. The dentist's wife had her dead husband's key copied onto a pink blank and still uses it. The high school has eleven keys for a building with six doors, and Alma has never found out which five are lies.

She works Saturdays alone. That's how she notices the Huang house. Number 14 Juniper, brass deadbolt, two years old, installed the week Mrs. Huang's mother moved in. In August someone brought in the same deadbolt, same wear on the cylinder, and asked for it to be rekeyed. The man gave the address as 14 Juniper.

Mrs. Huang did not come in. Mrs. Huang has come in for everything for two years, because Mrs. Huang does not trust her husband with keys, which Alma knows from the ledger and has never said out loud.

Alma writes *tell* next to the entry and cannot fill it in.

She walks past after closing. The lamp is on in the back room. The deadbolt is brass, two years old. She knows its sound the way you know a voice on the stairs — and it doesn't turn the way it should. It turns the way a new cylinder turns. Someone replaced a lock she made, in a house she inventories, and did it well enough that only the person who wrote the ledger would hear it.

She stands on the sidewalk with her bag of keys, in a town where she is the only one who knows how many doors there are, and understands that she has been reading this town for two years and it has been reading her back.

She goes home. She gets the notebook. She starts at the front.

**Thea Okonkwo, night cleaner, Ward 4, St. Bevan's Hospital.**

She has prosopagnosia: she cannot recognize faces, including the one in the mirror. She identifies people by voice, gait, the creak of a shoe, the sound a key makes in a pocket. She has worked the same ward for nineteen years, and she knows it better than the consultants who rotate through: which beds squeak, which night porter's steps pause outside the medication room, whose footsteps stop at room 12 and don't go in.

Everyone in the hospital treats her as furniture — a presence that empties bins and mops around the important things. That is exactly her advantage. She is in the room when nobody thinks to stop talking. She has heard the confessions, the affairs, the threats, the apology that came four minutes before the alarm.

Her method is sound, not sight. She can identify the person who came out of a room at 2:14 by the sound of a cough, or by whether they took the left corridor (which echoes) or the right (which doesn't). She has a memory like a wounded animal: total, involuntary, impossible to switch off.

The limits are real. She cannot pick anyone out of a lineup. She cannot say what someone looked like. She has been shown security footage dozens of times and has to be told who's in it. In court she is a witness no one wants, because everything she knows, she knows by ear.

She starts investigating for her own reasons: the night-shift porter she trusted for years — whose walk she'd know in her sleep — is the one she doesn't trust now. And nobody else will ask him anything. To them, he's a helpful man with a lanyard. To her, he's the one who came out of room 12 and didn't stop walking.

Name: Ines Varga, 41, night shift at a cold-storage depot for frozen blood plasma outside Szeged.

She counts. Not for pleasure. Her job is to reconcile the racks against the manifest every six hours, and she has done it so long that a wrong number reaches her before the thought does. A tray is missing a unit. A label reads one character off. She notices these the way some people notice a draft.

When a driver is found dead in the loading bay with no injury and a cooler bag beside him, the police ask the depot for a headcount. Ines is the only one who can give it, because she is the only one who remembers the racks as they were, not as the system says they are. The system says everything is correct. She says that is the problem.

She does not want to solve anything. She wants the numbers to close. Her method is to keep asking what should be there, and to be bothered by the answer until it is either found or explained. Other people in the story think of her as slow. She is only thorough in a direction they stopped walking.

Her weakness is that she trusts the count more than people. Her strength is that when the count and a person disagree, she goes back to the count first, and it has never once lied to her, only been misread.

Her name is Ondine Pak, and she cries for a living.

Twenty-two services last month. She stands in the back of chapels she has no claim to, in a black coat that is getting shiny at the elbows, and she does what the family paid for: weeps quietly enough to be respectable, loudly enough to be noticed. Two hundred a service, four hundred if they want the shaking shoulders. She has a card. She hands it out at funeral-home coffee urns, next to the bereavement caterers and the notary who does probate.

The work makes you good at rooms. Not at people—Ondine is bad at people, which is why the crying is easier than the talking. At rooms. She knows which pews have been reupholstered and which haven't. She knows the difference between a family that is sad and a family that is performing sad, and she knows that the difference is usually money. She knows that when a widow checks her watch during the eulogy, the will is already a war.

She started keeping a notebook because she kept seeing the same man.

He is not a mourner. He doesn't cry, doesn't sign the book, doesn't take a card. He arrives late and leaves before the recessional, and he stands at the exact spot where you can see both exits. Ondine noticed him the way she notices everything in a chapel: the way you notice a stain on the ceiling.

Eleven services now. Different cities within the county. A retired machinist, a teenage girl from a car on Route 9, a deacon, a man who owned three car washes. Ondine has a page for each one, and on each page, under the name and the date, she has written the same sentence: *he was here, and he was watching the ones who came alone.*

She has not gone to the police. What would she say? I was crying at a stranger's funeral, and there was a man. She is not a witness. She is a prop. Nobody in that room was looking at her except the family, and they were looking through her.

But here is the thing Ondine knows, and the thing she has not told anyone: at nine of the eleven, she saw the same woman too. Middle forties, good shoes. Never in the chapel—in the parking lot, in a car with the engine running, and once, at the deacon's service, standing in the rain without an umbrella, not getting wet the way people get wet when they're waiting for someone.

At the eleventh, the teenage girl's, the woman saw Ondine see her. She didn't look away. She raised one hand and touched her own collarbone, once, like someone checking for a necklace that wasn't there.

Ondine's next booking is Saturday. A retired schoolteacher, no immediate family, which means a small room and no one to hide behind. She has already decided she will not cry. She will stand where the exits are both visible and she will watch the door, and she will let the family keep their money.

She has one more page in the notebook. She's been leaving it blank for weeks because she doesn't know what to write on it, and because writing it would make it true: *they are not coming for the dead.*

Marisol Okonedo-Vance is forty-four and inspects pressure gauges for the Harrow Creek Water District, which serves eleven thousand people and three hundred and twelve pipe valves she can name from memory. She carries a clipboard with a clip that has been replaced twice. She does not carry a gun, a notebook full of theories, or a rumpled coat.

Her method is the logbook. Every station keeps a paper log, pencil in a waterproof sleeve, and she reads the entries against the numbers the sensors send to the district office. When the two disagree by more than the tolerance, she writes it down and drives out.

The first case she gets is small. Station 9, on the east slope, reports a steady nine-point-two pounds per square inch for six weeks, but the pencil log shows the same number written in the same slanted hand, and the day it changes, the handwriting changes too, a little more upright, as if someone wrote it slower on a cold morning. Nobody at the district signed for that shift.

She does not feel brilliant about it. She checks the valve tag, counts the bolts on the access hatch, and notices the hatch has been painted over twice, once in green and once in a grey that doesn't match. She writes that down too.

Marisol is not sure what the discrepancy means. She is sure it's real, because she has spent nineteen years learning the difference between a gauge that is wrong and a gauge that is lied to. Pressure can be faked. Pencil cannot, not without someone taking the time to copy it.

By the end of the week she has five more stations with the same upright handwriting, and a list of names on the sign-in sheets that do not match anyone currently on payroll. She does not call the sheriff. She puts the clipboard on the passenger seat, sets the logbook beside it, and drives to Station 9 again to look at the hatch from the inside.

.
- Default: a hardboiled or amateur-sleuth detective, or a quirky eccentric genius. Both are the obvious picks.
- Directions:
  1. Lens: a municipal parking enforcement officer who notices patterns in who never gets tickets. Grows from the fact that they walk the same streets daily.
  2. Material: a court stenographer who knows every lie by how it's typed. Grows from the fact that transcripts preserve pauses and hesitations.
  3. Subtraction: a retired piano tuner who hears a wrong note in the house where a death occurred. Grows from the fact that tuning requires patience and a trained ear.
- Pick: the stenographer. The hook is that she can prove a lie by its rhythm, and it fits a mystery because testimony is the central evidence.
- Reason: a mystery turns on what people say, and she is the person whose job is to hold every word exactly as spoken.

<final>
**Ruth Okonedo-Pell, 58, court reporter**

Ruth has taken down 41,000 pages of testimony over twenty-six years in the Dunmore County courthouse, and she has never once looked up from her machine to see who was lying. She doesn't need to. She hears it in the keys.

Witnesses who rehearse their stories type differently in her head. The sentences arrive too even, too tidy, with no false starts. Real memory stumbles. It doubles back, says "no, the Tuesday," corrects itself mid-clause. When Ruth transcribes a stumble, she marks it with a dash, and in twenty-six years she has learned that the dashes are where the truth lives.

She keeps a private ledger of these. Not for the court. For herself. Column one is the witness's name, column two is the sentence, column three is the place where the rhythm broke. Nobody reads the ledger. Ruth is a little embarrassed by it, the way some people are embarrassed by a bird they feed every morning.

She does not own a television. She eats lunch alone at the same counter, reading the menu the way other people read novels. She is the only person in the building who knows the judge's cough is a stall and not a symptom, because she has heard the judge's rhythm shift every time a lawyer approaches a sidebar he dislikes.

The case that breaks her quiet is a dull one: a dispute over a grain elevator lease, a clerk's accident, a chair with a loose leg. Then a witness named Desmond Vail takes the stand to testify about the night the clerk died, and Ruth's fingers stop on the third sentence. It is too smooth. It has no dashes at all. For the first time in twenty-six years, a perfect transcript makes her afraid.

She writes the sentence in her ledger and underlines it twice. Then she does something she has never done in her career: she asks the court for a copy of the audio.

Because the machine records everything, and Ruth knows what the machine cannot hear. What it can't hear is the thing she has been listening to all along: the silence before a lie, which is always a little too long.

Imagine your town has a vast number of messengers, and you can send one anywhere, instantly, without paying, any time of day.

You want to speak to your sister far away. You don't hand the messenger the letter; you hand them a copy. They leave with the copy and you keep the original, which is why nothing is ever lost from your own hands. If she wants to answer, she sends her own messenger back the same way.

Every person and every place that can send or receive has an address — jumbled letters and numbers nobody is meant to remember, like house numbers grown long and strange. When you tell your machine who to reach, other messengers work out the route the way a postal worker builds a path from your door through roads, another town's sorting room, and finally her street. No single messenger walks the whole path and knows the whole way. Each one knows only the next step.

Nothing travels as a solid thing. Your letter is broken into many small pages, and each page is sent on its own route; some arrive by one road, some by another, out of order. At her end the pages are gathered and put back in sequence, so a letter arrives whole even though it was carried in scraps.

The remarkably fast part is this: all of it, the copying, the routes, the reassembling, happens faster than a spoken sentence. And it isn't only letters. The same messengers can carry a photograph, a song, a voice itself — split the same way, rejoined the same way — so you can speak and hear your sister answer almost as if she stood in the room.

What you call "the internet" is not a place you visit. It is all these messengers and their roads, invisible, moving copies of what you send to anyone, anywhere, for no fare.

Think of the internet as the water in a town.

Somewhere far away there are wells — big buildings full of machines that hold things people have written, filmed or drawn. Those wells are what we call servers.

Under the streets run pipes. They are not one pipe. They are thousands of them, crossing and joining, and no one person owns all of them. When you ask for something — a photograph, a song, a page of writing — it does not come down the pipes as one bucket of water. It comes as thousands of cups. Each cup finds its own way through the streets. Some go left, some go right, some arrive late, and a few get lost and are sent again. At your house, the cups are tipped back into one jug in the right order, and what you see is a whole thing, not a mess.

The tap is the computer. The meter by the tap, if there is one, is what the phone company or the cable company charges you for — not the water itself.

Your house has a number. So does every other house, and every well. That number is how the water knows where to go. When you want water from a particular well, you say its number, and the cups set off toward you. If you don't know the number, you say the well's name instead — "the library on the hill" — and a town clerk's office somewhere looks up which number that name belongs to, then sends your cups the right way.

Two things to keep in mind. The water is not free of disease: some wells are run by people who want to take something from you, so you don't drink from every tap you pass. And the pipes don't care who you are. Anyone can put a cup in, and anyone can take one out. That is the whole reason it is useful and the whole reason it is dangerous, and it is the same fact both times.

Nia Okundaye assesses houses for a living. She works for the county's hoarding and neglect program, which means her week is a list of addresses and a set of tools: a moisture meter, a tablet, a box of shoe covers, a paint fan she uses to name colors in notes in case anyone asks her, later, to testify. Each house pays a flat fee. The route is set by dispatch. She has thirty-five minutes per property and a supervisor who flags her if she runs long.

Her skill isn't reading people. It's reading rooms. She has stood in something like nine thousand houses and she can date a room to about the week it stopped being lived in. The last clean sliver of countertop. The mail fanned on the floor, escalating from coupons to shutoff notices to nothing. The chair pulled to a window and pulled back. She is not sentimental about any of it, which is why she's good at it.

She isn't a detective and can't be one. Her reports are confidential, they travel between two departments, and after a write-up two years ago she was told plainly that anything she observes goes in the file and nowhere else. She carries a phone older than her car and she keeps the notes app empty.

The reason she's in this story: the coroner's office releases a name, and Nia has been inside that house before. Twenty-two months ago. She filed the assessment herself, and the report in the system is not the report she wrote.

Planning notes: The default protagonist here is the sharp, damaged detective with a secret — whiskey, insomnia, a dead partner. Next-most-obvious is the flip: a cheerful amateur, a nosy baker, a true-crime podcaster. Both are worn smooth. Thin request, short work — I should start from the material itself rather than my own taste, and since there's no project context, build a seedless but specific person rather than a genre archetype. Something where the mystery-solving ability comes from the job itself, and the job is unglamorous and real. Not a sleuth who happens to have a quirk — a person whose actual daily work produces the skill the plot needs.

Let me build from the fact rather than the vibe: who in the real world reads the same small inconsistencies for a living? Someone whose job is to notice that a thing doesn't belong where it is. Not a coroner, not a forensic expert — too expected. What about a person whose whole work is *putting things back where they were*, and who therefore notices when something has been moved? That has a reason: if your hands know the home position of ten thousand objects, you notice an object that's an inch off. That's the plausible mechanism.

Hmm, though — "notice things out of place" is itself a bit of a known detective trope (the obsessive-order person). The escape becoming a default. Let me move instead to a job where the noticing comes from *bodies of strangers treated the same way* — a person who handles the dead simply, at volume, without sentiment, in a place the mystery can't expect. A municipal mortuary attendant. But that's edging toward coroner/mortician, other-worldly gothic, which is its own cliché.

Better: pick a job where the protagonist's knowledge is about *texture and wear* and where money and complaints both flow — someone who sees people's private messes and cannot report them. An insurance loss adjuster? A mold remediator? Actually — a person whose job is assessing *hoarding and cluttered homes*, entering strangers' houses on a schedule, documenting what's there. Their skill: reading a house as a record of its occupant's last months. Nobody suspects them, they have legal entry to the home, and they know the truth because they've been in a thousand houses and can date a room to the week. That's specific, modern, unglamorous, and the protagonist cannot arrest anyone — they can only notice, which is exactly what a mystery needs and what makes it hard.

The character: not a hobbyist, not a know-it-all. Give them a real constraint — the job pays per case, they have a fixed route, a manager who watches productivity, and they are not allowed to talk about what they see. The protagonist's problem: they've been in the victim's house before and the report they filed contradicts what the house shows now. That gives the mystery a true reason to involve them and a real cost.

Details: the equipment — a moisture meter, clip-on booties, a tablet, a paint-swatch fan. The tell they use: the way a room is broken in the order a person stopped caring. Give them a body that's tired, not tragic. A reason they can't just call it in: privacy rules or a prior write-up.

Avoid: naming the feeling, three-item lists, a moral bow at the end, a title. Keep it in the user's language, English. Concrete, short sentences, varied length, ends by just stopping. One made-up fact risk: the job/pay details are plausible but invented — I'll keep them soft.

Move I'm taking: "protagonist with a routine, unsentimental day-job whose by-product is detective skill; mystery turns on a discrepancy in their own past paperwork." Check: could this be any project? The specificity of the clutter-assessment job ties it here. Is it the first thing most would make? No. Can I say why it fits? Yes — a mystery needs someone who notices contradictions; this job manufactures exactly that skill, and it lets the sleuth be outside the police rather than a rebel against them.

- Default: a hard-boiled detective, or a quirky amateur sleuth with a gimmick like being an ex-cop or a baker.
- Directions: (premise) a retired lighthouse keeper who reads tide charts as evidence; (lens) a court stenographer who knows everyone's lies by their pauses; (material) a conservator who restores paintings and reads crimes in the cracks of old varnish.
- Pick: the court stenographer. Strongest hook, and it fits a mystery because her whole job is recording what people say and noticing how they say it.
- Reason: a mystery needs someone who hears the gaps between statements, and a stenographer is paid to hear every word and forget none.

<final>
**Imogen Asker, 58, official court reporter, Division Four**

Imogen has taken down eleven thousand hours of testimony and has never once looked up from her machine to see a face. Her hands move; her ears do the rest. She knows a witness is lying not by what they say but by the half-second they spend on the word "always," and by the way a sentence loses its verb when the speaker is about to need one.

She keeps a private ledger of pauses. Nobody knows it exists. Each entry is a case she was never allowed to investigate: the attorney whose sighs ran longer before the stipulations that cost his client a retrial, the bailiff who coughed twice whenever a particular alibi was read. She has never been wrong enough to matter to anyone, which is its own kind of problem.

Her flaw is that she believes the record is complete. She trusts transcripts more than memories, and she has built her whole life on the idea that if a word was said in the room, it can be recovered. That faith makes her brilliant at finding what was said and blind to what was deliberately left unsaid, the silence someone planned for her to fill with her own assumptions.

She is precise in speech, slightly formal, and unsettlingly polite. She eats the same lunch at the same bench in the courthouse garden and counts the pigeons, out of habit, not sentiment. When she finally meets a case that is not in the record at all, a dead man's testimony that was never taken down, she has to decide whether to trust her ears or the thing she has always been sure of: that no one who speaks in a courtroom gets to disappear.

Imagine a very large apartment building. So large that nobody who lives in it has ever seen all of it, and nobody knows everyone. You live in one room. You want to ask a question of someone in another room, far away.

You can't walk there. The building is too big, and the halls twist. So you write your question on a piece of paper. You fold it, and on the outside you write where it should go. Then you slip it under your door into the hallway.

In the hallway there are people whose entire job is carrying paper. That's all they do, all day. One of them picks up your note. This carrier doesn't know the whole building either. He only knows a little: which way to go to reach the next hallway. He carries your note a short distance and hands it to another carrier, who knows a little more about that part of the building. That one hands it to another. The note gets passed along, room to room, hall to hall, until it reaches the person you named.

Here's the part that matters. If one hallway is blocked — a door stuck, a flood, a carrier who's sick — the note doesn't stop. The carriers just find another way around. There's always another path, because the building is woven together with hallways the way a cloth is woven with threads. No single hallway is the only way.

Sometimes your question is too big to fit on one piece of paper. So you tear it into many pieces, number them, and send each piece its own way. They may travel by completely different routes and arrive at different times. The person at the other end collects all the pieces and puts them back in order. If one piece is lost, she writes back and asks you to send just that piece again.

And some rooms aren't homes. They're storehouses — rooms full of shelves, where a note sits waiting. If you ask for something that's kept in a storehouse, the storehouse itself answers you, the same way a person would, by writing back. You don't know or care whether a person or a storehouse answered. All you know is a note came back.

So: the internet is that. Millions of rooms, no one in charge, no one who sees the whole thing. Just notes, addresses on the outside, and an enormous number of carriers who each know only their own small stretch of hallway — and who keep passing things along anyway, finding another way when one way is blocked.

The reason it keeps working is that no one has to know everything. Each carrier only has to know the next step.

Think of the internet as a library where nobody is allowed to walk to the shelves.

You sit at a desk by the door. You write what you want on a slip of paper, and you hand the slip to a runner. You never see the shelves. You have no idea which room your book is in, or which building, or which town. You just get a slip back, or a book.

Here is the part that surprises people. Nothing you ask for travels as one piece. Your request gets torn into small numbered pages, and each page goes out by a different runner, down whichever hallway happens to be moving that minute. Some go through the big downtown hall, some slip through back corridors, some go the long way around. Each page has the address of where it is headed written on it, and each runner only has to know the next doorway, not the whole journey. At the far end, a clerk collects whatever pages have arrived, puts them back in order, and if one is missing, sends a note asking for just that one page again.

Two things follow from this.

First, no single person anywhere understands the whole library. Not the clerks, not the runners, not the people who built the halls. Everyone knows their own doorway and the name of the next one. That is all it takes, multiplied a great many times.

Second, the library has no front door to close. There is no center to knock out. If a hallway collapses, the pages simply go a different way, maybe slower, and the desk at the far end waits a little longer. This is why it was built this way in the first place.

The desk you are sitting at is your computer. The card with your name and address that the clerk uses to send things back to you is what people call your connection. You do not own a piece of the library. You have a seat in it, and the seat has an address.

Who is the person you are explaining this to — someone elderly, someone from a village with no electricity, an office colleague?

Imagine a well in the middle of a town. Everyone needs water, but nobody wants to dig their own well, so the town keeps one, and everyone draws from it.

Now imagine that anything you might want to say or see is water. When you want some, you don't go to the well yourself. You ask, and a courier carries your bucket to the well, fills it, and brings it back. When a friend wants to send you water, they hand their bucket to a courier, and it travels the same way, arriving at your door.

The well is not one well. It is thousands of wells, all connected by the same set of roads, and the couriers know every road. So water drawn from a well across the ocean can reach your door in the time it takes to blink, because there are couriers standing at every corner, each one passing the bucket to the next.

Nobody owns the roads. Nobody owns the wells. The town agreed on the rules — how to address a bucket, how to hand it off, how to know it arrived — and then everyone built on top of those rules, which is why the town keeps growing and nobody had to ask permission.

And when the water arrives, it's only for you. The courier didn't read it. The next courier didn't either. They just carried.

That is the whole thing. A town that agreed to share its water, and a great many couriers who know the roads.

Now imagine that anything you might want to say or see is water. When you want some, you don't go to the well yourself. You ask, and a courier carries your bucket to the well, fills it, and brings it back. When a friend wants to send you water, they hand their bucket to a courier, and it travels the same way, arriving at your door.

The well is not one well. It is thousands of wells, all connected by the same set of roads, and the couriers know every road. So water drawn from a well across the ocean can reach your door in the time it takes to blink, because there are couriers standing at every corner, each one passing the bucket to the next.

Nobody owns the roads. Nobody owns the wells. The town agreed on the rules — how to address a bucket, how to hand it off, how to know it arrived — and then everyone built on top of those rules, which is why the town keeps growing and nobody had to ask permission.

And when the water arrives, it's only for you. The courier didn't read it. The next courier didn't either. They just carried.

That is the whole thing. A town that agreed to share its water, and a great many couriers who know the roads.

**Marisol Okonkwo-Reyes, 52, restorative cosmetician at Vance & Daughters Funeral Home, Dayton, Ohio**

Marisol has spent twenty-six years making the dead look like they are only resting. She reconstructs faces after car crashes with wax and tint, closes eyes that will not stay closed, and chooses lipstick shades for mothers who have not worn color in a decade. Her clients cannot thank her. Their families thank her, sometimes too much. She has learned that people remember a face the way they needed it to be, and she is good at giving them that.

She is also a quiet observer of the living, because the living bring her their worst hours. Widowers ask whether the bruise will show. Sons arrive with a list of what their father must not look like. Over the years she has learned to read the gap between what a family says about a person and what the body quietly reports: a wedding ring worn on the wrong hand, a shirt buttoned by someone in a hurry, a fresh scratch under a sleeve that the family insists was a fall.

She does not solve crimes on purpose. She notices, and she has been trained never to say what she notices out loud. That discipline is what makes her dangerous in a mystery. Detectives assume she is a witness; she assumes she is an interpreter. She keeps a ledger of small discrepancies in a green notebook, and she will not hand it over until she is sure the person asking is the one who needs to hear it.

**Opening scene (sample):**

The Halvorsen boy came in at nine on Tuesday with his father's good suit folded over one arm, as if he had brought the wrong size and was afraid of being told so.

"He's not vain," he said. "Don't do anything big."

Marisol nodded and took the suit. She had already seen the body by then, a fall from the loading dock of a warehouse, and she had already seen what the police report would not mention: the dead man's left hand had been scrubbed, hard, across the knuckles, and the skin there was raw, as though he had been trying to wash off something other than dirt.

She did not mention it. She laid the suit over the chair, asked the boy whether his father had preferred the blue tie or the grey, and wrote a single word in the green notebook: *Knuckles. Scrubbed after, not before.*

The boy chose the blue tie. Marisol made sure the knuckles did not show.
