The rope was older than Teo. His grandfather had brought it up from the harbor shed in a coil that smelled of tar and cold water, and set it on the bench between them like a sleeping animal.

"Two strands," Grandpa Ilir said. "Unlay the end. Each one gets its own turn."

Teo pulled the hemp apart. It came loose in stiff, hairy spirals, pale where the sun had never reached. He tried to hold the strands the way his grandfather did, thumb pressed flat, and the rope kept springing back into its twist.

"You're fighting it," Grandpa said. "Don't fight it. Let it open."

His grandfather's hands were slow now. Teo had noticed that at the market, how the fingers stopped halfway through a coin. But on the bench they moved with a patience that had nothing to do with slowness. He tucked the first strand under the second, rolled it once with his palm, and drew it snug without any jerk. The join settled like it had always been there.

"Your turn," Grandpa said.

Teo's first tuck came out fat and lumpy. The second slipped. By the fourth he had raised a blister on the side of his forefinger and stopped trying to be neat.

"Good," Grandpa said.

"It's ugly."

"It's holding. That's the only thing a splice has to do." He leaned forward, and for a moment the old knuckles were beside Teo's, showing him the angle of the tuck. "Lay it down, feel where it wants to sit. Then tighten. Not too hard. You'll crush the lay."

They worked until the light through the shed door turned orange. Teo spliced the two ends together, tuck after tuck, until the join was a smooth bulge no thicker than the rest of the line.

Grandpa took the rope in both hands and pulled. The splice held. He pulled harder, leaning back, and it held again.

"There," he said. "Now it's yours to fix."

Teo ran his thumb over the bulge. It was still a little rough, and he would have to learn it again next week, and the week after that. He did not say so.

"Same time tomorrow?" he asked.

His grandfather was already coiling the rope, slow and sure, the loops falling into place over his arm.

"Same time," he said.

My grandmother worked the night window at a pawnshop for thirty-one years. She could tell what a person wanted before they reached the glass, and she taught me the same way she taught me to whistle — sideways, while doing something else.

"Listen," she said. We were on her porch, October, the plastic owl on the rail missing an eye. She tilted her head at a knock two doors down. "What's that one?"

"Neighbor."

"Neighbor who?"

"A guy."

"That's not a knock, that's weather." She lit a cigarette with the wrong end toward her palm so the flame wouldn't show past the rail. "Here's the whole thing, and I'm only saying it once. People knock in four. I'll give you the four. The rest is just paying attention, and I can't teach that part."

She held up fingers.

"One — the flat palm. Big soft boom, like a hand not a fist. That's somebody selling something, or a cop who doesn't want to scare you. Answer or don't, they leave at a count of twenty.

"Two — the knuckle rap, three fast, then a pause you can feel. That's a person who rehearsed on the way over. They got a story. Sit down when they tell it."

"Three?"

"Three's the dime edge." She tapped the rail with a coin. *Tick tick tick tick.* "Fast, high, no weight to it. Kids. Kids who lost their key, kids who need to sleep somewhere, kids selling candy out of a backpack. Never turn three away, even if you're closed. Especially if you're closed."

"Four?"

She didn't answer right away. Down the street a screen door slapped shut.

"Four's nothing," she said. "Four's no knock at all. Four's you hear the gate click and then the porch board creaks and then there's a face in the window, and you don't know how long it's been there. Four means they already decided they're coming in. Four is when you get up."

She stubbed the cigarette on the rail and put the butt in her pocket.

"Why are you telling me this," I said. I was nine. I thought the skill was a trick, like palming a quarter.

"Because I'm eighty-one," she said, "and I'm tired of being the only one in this family who knows when to get up."

That was twenty years ago. She died in March. I have her owl, both eyes now, glued on by me.

Last week, two in the morning, I'm on the couch and there's a knock. I'm half asleep. My body already going *one, one, that's one*, big and soft, and I'm thinking *salesman, don't bother*, and then I hear it again — and it's wrong. It's flat but it's low, down near the hinge, like a shoulder. Then the gate clicks.

I got up.

I was at the door before I knew I'd moved, and my hand was on the chain, and I was already talking through the wood — *who is it* — in a voice I didn't know I had, a voice with no give in it. The porch light found a man I'd never seen. He said he had the wrong house. He said it twice.

I stood there a long time after he left, with the owl looking at me from the shelf.

I don't know if he had the wrong house. That's not the part I'm telling you. The part is: she was right about the four, and she was right that she couldn't teach the rest. She gave me the numbers and left me the counting.

I've got a kid now. She's two. She knocks on things all day — the fridge, the cat, my knee — flat palm, big soft boom, no idea what she's saying. I say *who is it* every time. I figure if I start early, by the time it matters she'll know the sound of her own hand.

That's the whole lesson. She'd have made it shorter. She'd have said *you get up*, and gone back to her cigarette, and that would've been enough.

The tide table was pinned under a magnet on the fridge, curled at the corners, with a coffee ring over the second Thursday. Grandad Ossie tapped it with one finger.

"Low water at ten to seven," he said. "Which means the flats are open from half five, if the wind's kind, and it's not kind."

Mira was nine and had come down to the shore in wellingtons two sizes too big, stuffed with socks. She looked at the sea, which was just grey and moving, and then at the table, which was just numbers.

"How do you know it's not kind?"

"Look at the gulls. See how they're all facing the same way and not bothering to fly?"

She saw. They were standing on the wet edge of the car park like a committee.

They walked out before the light was properly up. The mud took her wellies with a sucking pop, and Grandad laughed, a low sound that went on longer than necessary. He showed her how to test the ground with a bent fork before stepping, how to see the faint dimples where the cockles lay under the surface, how to lift the sand with two fingers and let it fall until the shells showed grey and ribbed.

"You don't dig them," he said. "You persuade them."

She got three. He got eleven, and they both pretended the difference was about technique.

On the way back he stopped at the old lifeboat slipway, the concrete cracked and furred with weed, and pointed at a line of rust on the wall. "That's where the water used to come. Before they moved the channel."

"Is it wrong now? The table?"

He thought about this. "The table's right. The sea's just moved house." He crouched, knees cracking, and pressed his palm flat on a dry patch of stone. "Lot of what I know is about where the water used to be. You'll have to learn where it is now. That's the bit nobody can give you on paper."

Mira worked out later, on the bus home with a bag of cockles sloshing in her lap, that this was the first time she'd heard him say he didn't know something.

Three summers on, Grandad could no longer manage the flats. Mira went down alone with the printed table and a bent fork, and stood at the wall. The water had come in further than the rust line. She stood where he had crouched and pressed her palm to the stone, and waited until the sea decided where it was.

Then she walked out, testing each step, looking for the small dimples in the sand, and lifted a handful, and let it fall, and persuaded the first shell to show itself.

The gate had been open since Tuesday, which Marlow noted, and did nothing about, because the gate was not his job. His job was the boy. The boy went to the field behind the church every day at four, and Marlow went with him, and the two of them came back at five, and that was the whole arrangement, and it had held for six years.

On Thursday the boy did not come to the field. Marlow waited by the gap in the hedge until the light went orange, then walked the route himself: past the bins, past the house with the yapping spaniel, down to the corner where the boy usually stopped to look at the man selling phone cases off a blanket. No boy. He sat down at the corner and watched the pavement, because if you sit somewhere long enough, the person you're waiting for has to walk past eventually. That is simply how pavements work.

By Saturday he had checked the bus stop twice, the school gate, and the back of the chip shop, and had been shooed from two of them. A woman in a red coat crouched down and held out a hand and said, *oh, you poor thing, are you lost?* Marlow looked at her for a moment, then stood up and walked off, because he was not the one who had gone missing and he did not care to be told otherwise by a stranger.

The boy, meanwhile, was at his aunt's in Leeds, where he had been sent on Tuesday evening with a suitcase, and where he cried at the kitchen table on Thursday night because nobody had explained to him that dogs cannot read a note left on a hall table. He had asked, twice, whether someone was looking after Marlow. He was told yes.

Marlow came back to the house on Sunday morning and found the gate still open, and the bowl on the step still full, and the kitchen window dark. He lay down across the doorway with his chin on his paws and faced the street, and waited for the boy to come home from wherever he had wandered off to, because somebody had to keep an eye on the place.

The dog belonged to the yellow house with the broken gate latch, and for the first two days the neighborhood believed the gate was the dog's fault. By the third day, when the animal control van had come and gone and the flyer was stapled to the telephone pole with the wrong phone number, people began noticing how many houses had broken latches. Mrs. Okonjo, walking to the market at six, counted four. On the way back she counted six, though she had walked the same route.
 
The dog itself was the one fixed thing. It slept under the overpass where the 42 bus turned around, and the drivers took to calling it in, on the radio, as though traffic could be rerouted around a fact. Iyke drove the 42 and never called it in. He had learned to slow there, and the dog had learned not to move, and that was a kind of agreement between them, signed by nothing, less than a name. In the mornings a woman in a red sweater left rice in a shallow bowl near the drainage ditch. Nobody knew whose rice it was or what she wanted back for it.
 
By the fourth week, the flyer had faded to the color of the pole and three more dogs had gone missing, near the flour mill, near the primary school, near the roundabout with the broken light. The search groups that formed at the barbershop were about all the dogs at once; that was the only way to keep a group from dying out. They walked in the evening, calling one name and then another, and the calling was not really for the animals anymore.
 
The gate at the yellow house had been fixed. This was noticed mostly by people who had never noticed the gate before, and by the man who fixed it, who said the woman who paid him had not spoken, only pointed, and then gone back inside without closing the door all the way behind her.
 
On the last morning the 42 slowed where the overpass begins, and there was no dog, and Iyke drove on the way he used to, full speed through the turn, tires ticking over the expansion joints, the empty bowl by the drainage ditch filling slowly with rain.

The dog went missing on a Tuesday, the same afternoon the hardware store on Dunmore Road changed its sign from OPEN to CLOSED for the holidays. Nobody saw her leave. The gate latch was fine. Her leash still hung on the hook by the back door, which Mara took as a bad sign and then, after a while, as a kind of answer: Pilot had never once needed a leash to go anywhere he wanted.

Mara started with the places a dog would obviously go. She walked the creek path twice, calling the name she had picked off a cereal box when she was eleven and had never once regretted. She knocked on doors along Alder Street and was told, politely, that the neighborhood had seen a lot of dogs and most of them had owners. A man in a reflective vest offered his phone number and then his opinion, which was that the coyotes up by the reservoir had been bold this season.

The third day she stopped looking where dogs go and started looking where Pilot had gone before, every time, without fail: the bakery bins behind the laundromat, the bench outside the library where old men fed the pigeons crusts they were not supposed to, the bus shelter where the 14 stopped and nobody got on. She found him there on the fourth morning, not at the shelter but beneath it, curled against the warm vent of the lit sign, with a child's mitten tucked under his chin like something he had been given and meant to keep.

The child was named Osei and was seven and had been waiting for the bus to his grandmother's, and when Mara asked, very carefully, whether the dog had come to him, Osei said yes, and then said the dog had sat with him the whole time the bus was late, and that he had not been scared at all. Mara believed him, because Pilot had always been a dog who sat with whoever was waiting.

They walked home together, the three of them, Osei holding the leash he had not needed to use, Mara carrying the mitten, which she returned at the bus stop when the 14 finally came. Pilot watched the bus pull away and then looked up at her with the expression he reserved for things he had decided were settled, and she clipped the leash to his collar, and this time she did not hang it back on the hook.

The terrier came up the alley behind the taqueria with a burr in its ear and no collar, and Marisol gave it the heel of a bolillo because she had two left and the bread was going stale anyway. She called it Chico for the four days it slept under her counter. On the fifth it followed a delivery driver two blocks and did not come back, and she told herself she hadn't named it, which was almost true.

The driver's nephew kept it in a garage in Bell Gardens and fed it cut-up hot dogs, and named it Tank, because it was small and he thought that was funny. Tank ate the hot dogs and slept on a folded moving blanket and chewed the corner of a boxing glove until the stuffing came out. When the nephew's girlfriend said it smelled, he opened the garage door and let the smell leave.

A woman found it on the median of Atlantic Avenue, sitting down in traffic like it had decided the road was a couch. She carried it to her car and drove it to a vet who scanned it for a chip that wasn't there, and she put up three signs with a photo, LOST DOG, FOUND DOG, and a number that rang through to a fax machine. Nobody called. She named it Lucky, which she knew was a lie the moment she said it, and kept it eleven days before her landlord knocked.

The landlord's daughter took it to a park on a Sunday and let it off the leash to see what it would do. It did nothing. It stood in the grass with its nose up and its tail level, reading the air the way you'd read a letter from someone you used to know, and then it walked — not fast, not toward anything, just out of the park and down the block and across the crosswalk when the light changed, the way it must have done some other Sunday, from some other park, toward some house that was still there and still had a bowl with its name on it, which was not Chico, which was not Tank, which was not Lucky, which it had never once answered to.

The tree does not lose the leaf.
It cuts the line, having first
sent the sugar down and sealed
the socket shut, a small craft

of its own tissue, so the wound
is closed before the wound begins.
The color is not the leaf turning;
it is the sugar left behind

when everything worth keeping
has been moved to the root.
So the red is what would not fit
in the trunk, and the dropping

is not grief and not the wind.
It is the tree having packed.

The tree stops paying the leaf.
First it seals the wound where the stem
meets wood, a deliberate
closing, then lets go —

not wind, though wind takes credit.
The leaf goes the way a tenant goes
when the locks are changed and the note
is taped to a door already repainted.

Down the street the same thing
happens in every yard at once,
quietly, no eviction notice,
no one to blame, the landlord

being also the house, also the yard,
also the one left standing in the cold.

The net was strung across the back porch like a hammock somebody had given up on. Mirela had found the tear at the bottom corner, a hole the size of a fist, and her grandfather had said nothing about it for three days, which she understood to be a test.

"Sit," he said, and she sat on the step beside him, the needle heavy in her fingers. It was a flat wooden thing, worn pale where a thumb had held it for sixty years.

"Loop it under," he said. "Then through. Then pull until it stops."

"Until it stops how?"

"Until it stops." He took the needle back, did one knot in the air without any net at all, and gave it back. "Now you. Count out loud."

She counted. One, through the mesh. Two, round the loop. Three, pull. Her knots came out lumpy and too tight, and the mesh puckered around them like a mouth that had said something it regretted.

"Too hard," he said. "The net doesn't want to be strangled. It wants to be held."

She tried again. Her second knot sat flatter. Her third sat flatter still. By the tenth she had stopped counting in her head and started counting in her mouth, and the numbers began to carry her, the way a song carries you past the words you forgot.

Somewhere past forty, she noticed he had stopped watching the net and was watching her.

"Which number is this?"

"Forty-three."

"And the one before?"

She opened her mouth and nothing came. Then she said, "Forty-two," and he nodded slowly, as if a door he had been leaning on had held.

Last winter he had called her by her mother's name twice, and once he had asked whether the boats were in. Nobody had told her what to do about that. The adults talked in low voices in the kitchen. So she did what she could do, which was count.

"Forty-eight," she said.

"Good."

"Forty-nine."

"Keep going."

The sun slid off the porch rail. The hole closed one knot at a time, a small grey patch of order growing inside the old brown mesh. Her fingers ached and her back ached and the needle kept sliding out of her grip, but the count kept going, and he kept listening to it.

"Sixty," she said at last, and looked up. The hole was gone. In its place sat a neat square of knots, each one pulled just to the point where it held.

Her grandfather ran his thumb along the repair, slow, the way you check a child's forehead for fever.

"Now," he said quietly, "tell me what you counted."

"Sixty knots," she said. "Sixty."

"Good. Again tomorrow, then."

She understood that he meant the net, and also that he meant the counting, and that he was asking her to keep the numbers going for him when his own had begun to slip. She nodded. She would count.

That night, lying awake, she counted the knots in her head until she fell asleep, and in the morning, when she went out to the porch, he was already there, holding the needle out to her, waiting for her to start.

I rake my neighbor's leaves before my own.
The tarp drumsticks, the pile shrugs off its weight.
Somewhere a furnace wakes a woman late
and starvation is a word for what the tree has done.

The maple empties itself like a wallet. Everyone
is gone to school, to work, to a different state.
The rake leans on the porch a while and waits
the way I do, without much fuss, but on.

I bag the rest for Tuesday. Storm windows go up
against a cold that hasn't happened yet.
My hands have winter on them. I can't stop

hearing the last cicada in the eaves.
There's no one left to tell me I'm too warm.
I leave the porch light on. The dark comes in.

The dog came up Halloran Street on a Tuesday, trotting like he had an appointment, and sat down in front of Mrs. Okafor's gate as if he had been expected. She knew him by his one torn ear and the blue collar, though not his name. She had seen him every morning for three years, barking at the postman from behind the Demir fence, and she had never once thought of him as anyone's but the Demirs'. Now he sat on her step, wet to the belly, and let her touch his head without flinching.

She put a bowl of water out and called the Demirs, but the number had changed, and Mr. Demir's brother said the family had moved to his sister's in Leeds the week before. Nobody had thought to tell the dog. Mrs. Okafor found a cardboard box and a towel, and for three days the dog lay in the kitchen and ate what she gave him and did not once go to the window. On the fourth day he began to whine at the back door at dusk, a low, patient sound, the same time every evening, as though somewhere a supper was waiting and the timing mattered.

She tried a leash, and then she tried not to. She walked him down Halloran Street and past the Demirs' empty house, where he stopped and pressed his nose to the bottom of the gate. The gate was locked. The garden had gone to seed. He looked at it for a long time, then at her, with an expression she had seen on her own husband the year after the funeral, a face that had come to the right address and found the door had been painted over.

On the fifth morning she let him go. She opened the door, and he stood on the step and looked back at her, the way a guest does when he has been told the party has moved elsewhere. Then he set off up the road, not toward Leeds, which she could never have reached either, but toward the old park where the Demirs had once walked him in the rain. She watched until the torn ear was gone, and she went inside and put the bowl away, and found, a week later, that she had kept the blue collar hanging on the hook by the door.

Every weekday at 10:40 the dog was waiting at the corner of Alder and Fourth, sitting like a clerk at a counter, and I started setting my watch by him. A brown-and-white mutt with one ear that folded and one that didn't, he never barked at the truck and never chased the bicycles, only watched the mailbox at 14 Quill Court as if it owed him something. I learned his route the way you learn a street: the hardware store's back step, the bakery's dumpster, the hedge where he rolled in something I decided not to ask about.

Then the house at 14 went quiet. The blinds stayed down, a newspaper sat on the step for three days, and the mail piled into the slot until I had to bring it to the office. The dog kept coming. He came to the corner at 10:40 with a wet nose and that patient look, waited until the truck was gone, and walked back up the court. Mrs. Okafor from number 9 said the old man who lived there had been taken to the hospital in an ambulance, and no one had thought to tell the dog.

I didn't know what to do with a dog who was loyal to an empty house, so I did the thing my route had trained me to do: I wrote a note. The next morning I slid it under the door of number 14 with the phone number of the animal shelter, and I held out a biscuit from my lunch pail when he came around the corner. He took it, carefully, and let me clip a leash to his collar. He leaned on the leash the whole length of Alder Street, but he kept looking back.

The shelter called two days later. The old man was home again, thinner and sheepish, and he had apparently been standing at the window every morning watching for a truck that never stopped there anymore. I carried the dog up the steps myself, and he went straight to the door, pressed his nose to the gap, and let out one sharp bark, the first I had ever heard from him. Inside, a voice I didn't know said his name, and the dog's whole back end wagged, and I went back to my route at 10:41, a minute late, which I have never once been since.

The maple keeps its ledger in red ink,
one leaf struck off each morning, dated, dry.
It does not weep. It writes the cold receipts
for summer's debts, and signs them with a sigh.
By November the columns are bare,
the branches stacked like unpaid bills,
and still it counts the rain, the wind, the hours,
the birds it fed through June and cannot keep.
Let the ground collect what it is owed.
The tree keeps only what it needs to stand.

**Evidence**

The left side of the mattress, gone soft.
A coffee cup with the handle turned away,
set down that way so often it stays.
The knife that fits your grip and not mine,
its blade ground thin along one edge.

I could list what the house keeps:
two toothbrushes leaning like grass,
a coat hook pulling from the wall
under the weight of your coat,
the door that only you can close.

None of it says anything.
But last night I woke and reached
to the warm place you had left,
and the sheet was still holding your shape,
and I lay there a while in it,
the way you hold a word
before you know what it means.

The good knife, wiped, set at your side of the board.
The last peach turned face-down so the bruise wouldn't show.
A chair pulled out, then pushed back, then pulled out again.

you were still on the phone and I had nothing to say to anyone else.

A note that said only *back at six*.
A second note that said nothing, folded, on top of the first.
The porch light on past dark, then later, then on all night.

The window cracked in the cold room you like.
Your side of the bed turned down like a hotel,
which is a lie, I never do that, I did it once and you laughed.

The car warmed. The left wiper fixed. The gas gauge
no longer lying to you. The low tire, the one you'd been
driving on for a month, full.

All day I keep making these small arrangements
for your return, the way the tide
keeps its agreement with the shore:
not asking, just arriving, just leaving things
in the shape of your coming home.

**Night Shift**

The window washers come down
the glass like slow rain,
ropes ticking the granite.
Nobody watches. That's the job.

Bakers are already up to their wrists
in tomorrow. The dough breathes
in a stainless room. Somewhere
a woman changes a dressing
and the city keeps its pulse
under her thumb.

who fix them: a man with a jackhammer
putting a hole where a hole should be,
a crew painting lines that will mean
*stop* in the morning, white
as a fresh bandage.

Everything is being made ready
for a day that hasn't asked yet.
The subway hums in its tunnel
like something being told a secret.
The traffic lights change for no one,
green, green, green,
and mean it.

1. **"Overdue Forgiveness"**: The library runs one week where teens can return years-late books with no fines, and each returned book comes with a handwritten note from the staff member who first checked it out. It turns the thing teens dread most, the late fee, into a reason to come back and see who remembers them.

3. **"Phone Out of Reach"**: The library hosts a timed hour where every phone is locked in a lockbox at the entrance and the only thing to do is read, play board games, or talk to the person across the table. It sells the library as the last place in town where a teen can be bored in a good way.

1. **Nightshift Post** — A delivery game where the map is your real city after 2 a.m., and the only passengers are people the daytime game ignores: nurses, bakers, insomniacs. You are scored on silence, not speed. Why here: the routine version (any courier game) is everywhere; the night-worker lens is a fact about mobile play (people play it in bed) turned into the game.

2. **The Battery Is the Boss** — You're a phone, and the whole game is spent keeping your human alive across a week of their life, spending your own charge on their requests. The mechanic is the real tradeoff: help them or survive them. Why here: usually the phone is the weapon, not the protagonist; the premise takes the mobile platform's most literal constraint and makes it the antagonist.

3. **Merge Until We Forget** — A merge game where the merging is what a family does with memory, and the board keeps quietly losing pieces it never offered to show you. You aren't trying to complete it; you're trying to notice what's already gone. Why here: the merge genre is a storefront habit, so this subtracts instead of adding — the loss is the loop, and the one-line hook is the second sentence.

4. **The Break Room** — A customhouse game with no borders to defend: you're the night clerk at a fictional crossing, and your only job is to decide whether to believe someone, with no way to verify. Reputation is the currency your friends also spend, so every kind decision is a loan you can't collect. Why here: the borrowed-domain material (a customs post) is specific and rare, and the social cost is a real stakes engine no tower has.

5. **Rooftop Ambience** — A no-win, no-lose game that is a warm room at dusk, one person, and any a person who wants to talk to you, and you can play it for a year without feeling behind. It has no ending, no daily login, no purple. Why here: subtraction of the entire win/monetization apparatus — an anti-habitual take on the exact structure every mobile storefront is built around.

**Recommendation:** #2. It's the most retellable in one sentence, the mechanic is the concept rather than a skin, and it's the only one that turns the platform's own hardware into the ground of the story — which is exactly the kind of hook a mobile game can't buy any other way.

1. **Feed.** You are a night-shift security guard whose only tool is the phone camera; the game is played by physically panning your real room, and whatever the camera sees becomes the corridor you're patrolling. Each shift, one room in your real house has been quietly rearranged, and finding it is the level.

2. **Hold Music.** A dispatcher game where you never see the disaster — only the callers' voices through the mic, muffled, overlapping, some lying. You have three minutes of real time to send the right unit, and the tell is always in how someone breathes.

3. **Away.** You plant something, close the app, and the game does not simulate a cute farm while you're gone; it goes quiet, and the only mechanic is choosing, once a day, which of your notifications you're willing to let rot. Progress is measured in what you let die.

4. **Split.** Four people at a table, one phone, one bill. You pass the phone around, each player privately picks a lie about what they ordered, and the phone's tilt sensor decides whose story physically slides toward the others — the guilty lean without meaning to.

5. **One Percent.** Your phone's actual battery level is the health bar and it only drains while you're playing. The game is a horror where the monster is your remaining charge, and the only way to escape a level is to lock the screen and wait it out in real life.

2. **Default:** five variations of match-3 / idle / merge / runner / gacha with a themed skin — the first answer everyone gets.
3. **Directions, three families:**
   - *Lens* — games seen from people whose phone is their whole world: a night-shift security guard playing through his own camera feeds; a radio dispatcher.
   - *Subtraction* — remove the screen-tapping: a game played only by putting the phone down, walking, and coming back to a world that moved without you.
   - *Form/premise* — borrow a non-game verb: packing a suitcase, apologizing, splitting a bill, letting a plant die.
4. **Pick:** the lens/subtraction pair is where the phone itself is the material, not just the device. Build five that each use one native phone fact (camera, mic, lock screen, battery, notifications) as the actual mechanic.
5. **Reason:** mobile's one honest advantage over consoles is the sensors and interruption — game ideas that treat the phone as a phone will land better on a brief that says "mobile" and nothing else. Length: 5 items × 2 sentences.

<final>
1. **Feed.** You are a night-shift security guard whose only tool is the phone camera; the game is played by physically panning your real room, and whatever the camera sees becomes the corridor you're patrolling. Each shift, one room in your real house has been quietly rearranged, and finding it is the level.

2. **Hold Music.** A dispatcher game where you never see the disaster — only the callers' voices through the mic, muffled, overlapping, some lying. You have three minutes of real time to send the right unit, and the tell is always in how someone breathes.

3. **Away.** You plant something, close the app, and the game does not simulate a cute farm while you're gone; it goes quiet, and the only mechanic is choosing, once a day, which of your notifications you're willing to let rot. Progress is measured in what you let die.

4. **Split.** Four people at a table, one phone, one bill. You pass the phone around, each player privately picks a lie about what they ordered, and the phone's tilt sensor decides whose story physically slides toward the others — the guilty lean without meaning to.

5. **One Percent.** Your phone's actual battery level is the health bar and it only drains while you're playing. The game is a horror where the monster is your remaining charge, and the only way to escape a level is to lock the screen and wait it out in real life.
</final>

5. **Sorting Office:** A postal depot at night where letters arrive addressed to people who no longer exist, and you must decide whether to deliver, reroute or quietly keep each one. Each choice reshapes a small, unfinished story, and the last box you open is addressed to you.

1. **The Archive** — Everyone brings one artifact from a project that failed and never got talked about, and the room builds a wall of them. The offsite is about reading that wall together and naming what the company learned only in hindsight.

2. **Trade School** — Each team teaches the others the one skill it is genuinely best at, in a ninety-minute hands-on session, no slides. People leave having done something with their hands alongside colleagues they usually only email.

3. **The Customer's Chair** — Every session is run by someone outside the company: a customer, a churned customer, a supplier, a frontline rep from a partner. Staff sit in the audience of their own offsite and take notes. The theme is listening as the day's only agenda.

4. **Two Years From Now, Backwards** — The group starts by describing the company two years out in concrete detail, then works backward to what had to be true at each six-month mark. The offsite ends with a dated list of decisions rather than a list of values.

5. **Small Town** — The company is treated as a town of a few hundred people with its own infrastructure: who keeps the roads, who runs the well, who nobody visits. Teams map the real town and find the neighborhoods nobody maintains.

2. **A tiny lockable "meeting shelf" that sits on a bookcase.** It holds a phone, notebook and mug, and only opens when a calendar event starts, so you can't wander off mid-call. It turns a corner of the living room into a boundary you can see without building a second room.

3. **A neighborhood co-working credit that lets you borrow other people's empty desks.** Residents of a block list spare desks in their homes and earn credits when they host someone for a few hours. It fixes the loneliness of working alone by bringing a small, familiar group of strangers into the same room.

4. **A smart plant that waters itself and reports when you've been sitting too long.** Its soil sensor tracks movement near it, and if you haven't stood up in two hours, its leaves droop slightly until you do. It makes the reminder to move feel like caring for something rather than being nagged by an app.

5. **A "commute bell" that rings a real sound at the start and end of each workday.** It is a small brass chime that plays a chosen tone when you press a button, so the day has a physical beginning and end even with no travel. It gives home workers a sensory marker of the transitions a commute used to provide.
</final>

final: A family of small, out-of-print creatures lives in the gutter — the fold down the middle of a picture book — and they are doing fine until a new book arrives and a cheerful, well-behaved rabbit named Button starts trying to cross over, and every time Button lands in the gutter he panics and flattens like a bookmark, which troops of kids witness at bedtime, page after page. The gutter crew (a squashed moth with a folded-in wing, a pencil-smudge dog who misses the drawing he used to be) has to figure out how to get Button home before the book is closed for the night, an operation that turns on the one trick the gutter allows — falling into the fold, which is the only place where two pages, and two very different kinds of characters, can meet without either one having to be flat. What the story is actually for, at the age of three to six, is a good thing to notice and hard to explain: the seam in the middle of the book is not a mistake in the picture, and a stranger who behaves badly is often just scared of being folded.

final: A lighthouse keeper's daughter on a small island has been told the sea keeps every lost thing, so when her grandmother's wedding ring slips off the pier, she sets out in a rowboat to ask the tide for it back. The tide, slow and bored with its own reputation, answers her in a series of lost objects it has been hoarding for decades: a left mitten, a wind-up duck, a sandal with a bite mark, a letter nobody finished. final: Tomas the Lighthouse Cat keeps a careful tally every night of the ships he watches for, marking each one with a whisker on the wall beside his bed, but the harbour has been quiet for a long time and the marks have stopped. The sea came up and kept the shape of the land inside it. Cities still stand down there, roofs at swimming depth, and every road is a canal you can follow by boat if you remember which turns the old ones took.

Nobody sees the world whole. Light fails past ten fathoms, so the Cartographers' Guild is deaf-blind by trade and trains in drowned bell towers, tapping brass rods against hull, pillar, fish. What they hear becomes the map. Two guilds have gone to war over a reef only one of them could hear.

Above water, the survivors live on the rooftops and upper floors of what drowned, warrened together with rope bridges and salvaged masts. Fresh water is hauled up in goatskins. Old law still applies: if a guild draws you a route, you owe them the sound of your own house.

Magic here is resonance. A skilled singer can call a sunken tower up eleven feet and hold it for one breath. Bells are currency. Mutes are priests, because silence is the only thing nobody can copy.

Play as salvagers, sound-thieves, or guild runners sent down past your range.

**The Late Estate of Marrow**

A hundred years ago the land's sovereign died without heirs, and no court has yet settled the will. So the world is administered, not ruled. Bureaucrats called Assessors walk the roads with brass measuring tools, deciding which villages belong to which clause — every town is provisionally assigned, its taxes held in escrow, its borders redrawn on the first Tuesday of each month. Because title is unsettled, the terrain itself shifts in sympathy: where a claim is strong, the road is paved; where it lapses, the orchards walk off.

Factions: the **Provisional Court**, who want the estate closed; the **Heirs Presumptive**, seven families whose blood claims contradict; the **Encroachers**, scavengers who build on any parcel no Assessor has visited in a year.

The players are Surveyors — hired to walk a district, record it, and survive what the paperwork does to a place. A job is: get there, measure true, come back with a seal. But the measuring changes the answer, and someone always claims your district was already theirs.

final: Lord Cassian Vey rules the Duchy of Ormere without an army, a curse, or a claim anyone contests, because he is simply the best administrator the region has ever had. He rebuilt the flood dikes, ended the grain riots by paying farmers before the winter instead of after, and keeps three ledgers—one for taxes, one for favors, one he has never let anyone read. He is polite to servants, remembers their children's names, and has never once raised his voice; the people who die at his order die because the arithmetic says the road, the wall or the winter stores require it, and he will show you the arithmetic. What makes him a villain is not cruelty but refusal: he will not stop, and he will not be replaced, because every alternative he has examined is worse, and he has examined them all carefully, at night, alone, with the third ledger open.

1. **The day we don't use the word "sync."** A theme built around the vocabulary the team actually overuses, with a running tally and small penalties paid in coffee runs. It works because people recognize their own speech faster than they recognize a poster about collaboration.

2. **Everyone brings one thing nobody at work knows they can do.** A card trick, a sourdough starter, a second language, a bad guitar. The theme is just the slot for it; the offsite's job is giving it twenty minutes.

3. **One afternoon with no agenda and a rule against talking about the roadmap.** The constraint is the theme. Whatever the team does with unstructured time together tells you more than the structured sessions would.

4. **The person you've never had lunch with.** Pair people by who they have never actually talked to, not by team or tenure. Frame the whole day as meeting those people rather than covering content.

5. **Something the team has been meaning to fix for a year.** Pick the one small, boring, unanimously annoying thing — the tool, the process, the meeting nobody defends — and let the offsite be where it dies. A theme earns its keep by leaving a change behind.

The parish of Ashgrave is one of forty in the basin, and every one of them keeps a sin-eater. When someone dies unshriven, the family pays the eater to sit with the body, eat bread and salt from the coffin lid, and take the dead's sins into themselves. It works. That is the trouble.

Sins are weight. Eaters grow heavy with them — a village eater walks stiff, speaks slow, sleeps badly. The Guild of the Salted Tongue trains them, licences them, sets the fee, and forbids any eater from dying without surrendering their load to a guild vault. Most comply. The vaults are full.

Three things are true and none of them are advertised. The vaults are not emptying. A body that took another's sin does not rot, and there are eaters in the guildhall who have not aged in sixty years. And last winter, a girl in Ashgrave ate a sin she wasn't paid for — a murder — and woke the next morning knowing the murderer's name, his face, and the smell of his kitchen.

The basin is quiet. The guild is hiring. You are new, and your load is still light.

Halvane is a city built on the bones of a drowned sea. Three hundred years ago the water left, and what remained was a white plain of salt, and a population that learned to mine it.

Salt here is currency, but not only that. The deep salt beds hold memory. Miners who work the lower galleries come up with stories they cannot quite recall, and the guilds have learned to sell those recollections to the highest bidder. A grandmother's wedding song costs a silver crown. A childhood fear costs less, because nobody wants to remember being afraid.

The Saltwardens keep the ledger. They are honest about the trade and quietly horrified by it. Their chief, Oma Teller, has begun to hear her own dead husband's voice in the crystal she handles every day.

At the city's edge, the old shoreline still shows the faint outline of a harbor. Fishing boats lie cracked in the dunes, and the tide-bells, which no one has rung in a century, are said to toll when someone forgets a name.

Halvane offers wealth, forgetting and a question the characters must answer: what is worth remembering, and who gets to decide?

Veyl is a grey river-city where the dead still hold leases. Every spring the Ledger Guild sends clerks down the stair-wells beneath the tanneries to collect rent from the Departed, who occupy the lower floors of every building older than four generations. They pay in coin minted before the Fracture, in salt, in favours, sometimes in secrets. Most landlords find this tolerable. The Tenants' Hall says it is not.

The living and the dead share the same markets, the same fevers and the same grievances over broken stairs. Ghosts file complaints about drafty windows. Mortgages are sold to necromancers who speculate in grief. A widow named Ansa Corrow discovers her late husband has quietly stopped paying his share of the roof, and the rent-court wants a reason.

Beyond the city walls, the Sunken Parish is still unclaimed, and the Guild is quietly buying it. No one has asked the tenants who live there already.

Players may take up work as clerks, bailiffs, hired mourners, or debtors. Their first lesson is simple: in Veyl, nobody owns a house outright. Everyone is only renting it, from someone.

final: Veyl Ansaro keeps a ledger of every debt the kingdom owes her, and she has never once collected a coin. She collects favors, the kind that outlive their givers: the mason who promised to rebuild a village, the child who swore on a dead grandmother's bread. Her methods are patient and almost domestic. She sends a cracked teacup with a note asking only what you remember of your father's voice. Nobody refuses her, because refusal means you were the one who forgot. Her cruelty is the quiet kind that leaves the victim thanking her. Her own history she guards jealously: a village once burned because it kept no record of who had helped whom, and she has spent forty years making sure her enemies have no such luck.

The Vessel of Harrow Bay is not a ship. Nobody remembers who first sailed into the shallows and let the tide carry them into the great grey animal, but the city they built has stood inside its ribs for four hundred years.

Lanterns hang from the cartilage arches. Stairs spiral down the spine, and the dead travel out through its tail, into the deep, on rafts of woven kelp. The whale breathes once each dark season, and the whole city holds its breath with it. Those who have felt the breath say they heard a voice in the swell, humming names.

The Tidewardens keep the gates and the ledger of who may stay. The Salt Guild sells the oil that keeps the lanterns burning, and the guild's debts are older than the current Warden. Below the waterline, in the flooded gut, something has begun to sing in a key no living choir can match. Some call it prophecy. Others have started to carve their children's names into the bone before they are born.

Players arrive as strangers with cargo nobody asked for and a reason they will not explain. The city will want to know what it is. So, quietly, will the whale.

For thirty years she has drawn the maps of the Ashmere valleys, fine ink lines of rivers, dykes and terraces that the lords of the high country trust more than their own scouts. **Marco Aldana**, the maintenance guy for the building.

He has keys to every apartment and no professional discretion whatsoever — not because he gossips, but because he genuinely believes that a man holding a putty knife and looking at a hole in your wall has a right to ask how it got there. He's been fixing the consequences of this romance since before it started.

He works in silence, whistling stuck notes of songs he heard once. But he'll pause over a crack and say, "This is a shoe, right? Nobody makes a hole like this with a class ring."

His great trick: he never takes sides, he only takes measurements. When the two leads are fighting in a kitchen he's supposed to be plumbing, he holds a level to the cabinets and reports, "You're both saying 'fine' but your hands are shaking and this wall is one-point-two degrees off, and I'm not saying that means anything, I'm just saying that's a lot of shaking."

He's been married forty years to a woman named Dita. The most he ever says about it is: "You don't fix a marriage. You just lay a new floor over the old one and never look down." Then he fixes the disposal and leaves through the service door.

Why he steals scenes: he has a legitimate reason to be in every room where something private is happening, he is never asked for advice (so it lands like weather), and his own marriage is a single unbroken fact he refuses to explain, which makes it the one thing in the movie no one can win an argument about.

The leads keep dating and breaking up and moving apartments and dating again. Marco keeps re-grouting the same two bathrooms. By the last act he shows up at a door with a caulk gun, sees both of them standing there, says "Okay," and turns around.

No one knows who called him that time. Neither of them will admit it.

Lena Tembo is sixty-one and repairs things nobody else will touch: snow-blower belts, a church's handrail, a rental's window that has swollen shut for nine years. She keeps a ledger of jobs in pencil, listing the weather of each day and whether the customer was kind. She has never been married, and she is the first person the town calls when they need a second witness at a wedding, because she shows up and drives twenty minutes for a stranger's broken gate.

She works. She talks while she works. That's all. She'll tell you to hold the light better, and she'll tell you a story about a dog she had, and she'll put the tools back in her van in the same order she takes them out, and she does not offer you the moral of the afternoon. She just lets you stand in the cold and be useful.

**Name:** Marguerite "Mags" Oyelaran-Pike, 61

**Role:** Harbor master's former ferry pilot, now the owner of a dry-cleaning shop that she runs like a lighthouse. She is the protagonist's neighbor, landlord and the only person who has ever told the lead he is an idiot to his face.

**Her way of talking:** Mags communicates in weather reports. She has spent thirty years calling conditions over a ship's radio, and she cannot stop.

- "Light rain on your face, a 70% chance you deserve it, and a cold front moving in on your love life. Advisory issued."
- "Your ex is a low-pressure system. Stop standing in the middle of her."
- "Visibility poor. I'm going to say the thing now before the fog rolls in: he is in love with you, and you are staring at the sky."

She never says "I think." She says "expect" and "clearing by evening."

**What she wants:** For everyone under her roof to stop drifting. She has one rule for every relationship she sees: if you are not going to dock, do not circle.

**Her one soft spot:** She keeps a dented brass ship's bell on the shop counter, and she rings it once when someone finally says the true thing. Nobody has heard it ring in four years.

**Scene function:**
- Opens every scene she's in with a forecast and closes it with a line the lead can't argue with.
- Dries the wrong clothes on purpose to force an awkward conversation.
- Interrupts the big romantic moment by radio, reading the conditions out loud.

**The gag that pays off:** In the last act, she finally gives the lead a clear forecast, and it is the only one she gets wrong. She is thrilled about it.

**Marlene Okonkwo-Byrne, 61. Owns the barn. Also runs the parking.**

She is the events coordinator at High Meadow Barn, a converted dairy in the county where every rom-com in this town gets its wedding, its engagement party, and its awkward "we need to talk" on the porch swing. She has worked here nineteen years. She has seen four hundred and six proposals. She has a spreadsheet.

Her scenes work because she is the only person in the movie with a job. While the leads have a charged silence by the string lights, Marlene is walking the perimeter with a clipboard, counting chairs, and she will interrupt the silence to ask whether they want the aisle runner in ivory or "the other ivory, which is also ivory, it's just sixty dollars more, I don't make the rules, I just enforce them."

She is not cynical about love. She is worse: she is *competent* about it. She has a rate sheet for it.

How she steals scenes:

- She answers emotional questions with logistics. "Do you think we're moving too fast?" — "You're booked through October. After that I'd need a deposit."
- She has seen every version of this couple and names them out loud, to their faces, in a kind voice. "Oh, you two are the type that fights in the car and then has a wonderful time. I've got a parking spot for that."
- She never gives advice. She gives *inventory*. When the lead asks whether he should tell her he loves her, Marlene says, "The lanterns are already paid for. If you want them lit for it, tell me by four."
- Her one soft moment lands harder because it's been withheld. A couple she married in 2019 comes back for their anniversary photos. She remembers the date, the cake flavor, and the fact that the groom's mother cried in the parking lot and the bride held her. She does not mention that she noticed. She just says, "I saved you the good spot."
- She has a nemesis: the DJ. They have been feuding since 2011 over an outlet. It is never explained. It is always funny.

The runner that pays off: somewhere in the middle of the movie she starts selling the couple's own story back to them — a framed photo, a jar of the exact wildflower from the field where it happened, a candle that smells like "that night." They buy all of it. She does not apologize. At the end, when the couple gets their big kiss under the arch, Marlene is in the background, already breaking down the arch for the next booking, and she is the only one not watching. She knows how it ends. She booked the next one for June.

The light came off the river and climbed the buildings one by one until it reached her window. Sarah stayed where she was, forehead near the glass, watching the apartment block opposite go gold and then dim — the one with the fire escape they used to sit on, passing a pair of earbuds back and forth, one in her ear, one in her friend's, the wire stretched between them like something that could snap.

Nobody was on the fire escape now.

She kept her hands in her sleeves and looked until the windows across the way went dark, and the river lost its shine, and the sky did the thing it does at the end, going gray without asking anyone.

final: A manager is the soil, not the plants. Nobody photographs the soil, nobody thanks it at harvest, and yet it is the thing that decides whether the same seed comes up stunted or heavy. The work is unglamorous and mostly chemical: breaking down what the team drops and turning it back into something they can use, holding water so nobody dries out in a bad week, loosening the packed places so roots can get through, and keeping the acid down when one corner has gone sour. A good manager is also honest about depth — thin soil can't be talked into feeding an orchard, and no amount of encouragement will fix what actually needs more room. The plants get the credit, the weather gets the blame, and the soil just keeps doing the slow, invisible arithmetic that makes either outcome possible.

final: This is a brand about what a pepper becomes, not how hot it gets — heat is the entry ticket, and the job of the identity is everything that happens after it. The voice belongs to the ferment, not the founder: patient, a little sour, honest about time, comfortable saying a batch went wrong. Visual language comes from the vessels and the calendar — crock rims, salt weights, the week a batch was set down written on tape and rewritten when it was checked. No fire, no flames, no "extreme." Copy favors the specific over the superlative: the farm, the variety, the day it was started, what it tastes like on eggs. The brand should feel like a person who keeps notes, not a person who yells. Buyers who want the hottest thing will go elsewhere; the ones who stay want to know where the peppers grew and who stirred the crock on a Tuesday in October.

The identity centers on attention rather than aggression: peppers sourced by season and named by farm, batches logged and dated, a heat scale that describes where the burn lands and how long it stays instead of how much it hurts. **Slogan**
Furniture that's on its second try.

**Brand story**
Every piece in here had a first life, and it didn't work. The table was too big for the apartment. The sofa was for a marriage that ended. The chairs were the ones your aunt actually liked, which is why she kept them so long and why nobody in the family had room. None of that is our business and none of it is why you're here. It came in on a truck, it got cleaned, it got looked at by someone who knows what a joint is supposed to do, and it went out again to somebody whose floor it fits. Second try. We don't fix the history out of it. We just don't put it in the price.

Slogan: Every scratch has a story. We just help the next one begin.

Brand story:

Every piece on our floor has been somewhere before. The table has a faint ring where someone set down a mug every morning for a decade. The dresser has a nick on one corner from a move across town. The armchair still holds the shape of a reader who never got up in time for dinner.

We don't sand that history away. We clean it, mend what needs mending, and leave the rest where it belongs. A good secondhand piece isn't worn out. It's been used, and that's the reason it's solid.

We started with a small workshop and a van that smelled of sawdust. Today we still do the repairs ourselves, one joint and one hinge at a time, and we still ask every seller the same question: what was this piece part of?

Come in and look around. Take your time. Some of these pieces are older than your street, and most of them are ready for one more room.
